A SWING SONG. Dew little maid in the garden so fair, Swinging away in the old oak swing, ft Backwards and forwards, now high, now low, k, What is the song that it seems to sing? r- "Be good, sweet maid, at work or at play, And waste not an hour of the fleeting day." ik Dear little maid, the wee birds overhead tr.,. Are joyously trilling a carol sweet, -I.• Filling with music the sunshiny air. What are the words the birdies repeat? "e good, sweet maid, at work or at play, ft And waste not an hour of the fleeting day." Fr" Dear little maid, through the shady green trees, Stirring their branches, the breezes blow, 14 And ever and aye to your listening ear The same refrain they softly echo: "Be good, sweet maid, at work or at play, And waste not an hour of.the fleeting day." •Little Folks" Magazine, for June. • t • A -.•-•

r • JUNE DAYS. The whilom hills of gray, whose tender shades • Were dashed with meagre tints of early Spring, Lift now/their rustling domes and colonnades, And from the airy battlements they fling r Their banners to the wind, and in the glades Spread rich pavilions for the Summer's king. r Now lifts the love-lit soul, and life's full tide Swells from the ground and beats the trembling air, Mounts up the steeps, and on the landscape wide Spreads like a boundless ocean everywhere, Delight's dear dreams the dancing waves divide, And with swift sails outtly pursuing Care. The sometime fields that sad and sodden lay, Soaked in the first cold rains, or flecked with snow, ' With helpless grasses trodden in the clay By shivering herds that wandered to and fro, Wave now with grain, and happy birds all day Pipe, hidden on the slopes with flowers ablow. The yellow streams that fled from Winter's hold I,x,en first the young year saw the vernal moon, And lipped the yielding banks whose moistened mould Slipped mingling with the flood, now sleep at noon, Calm as the imaged hills which they enfold, All glimmering in the long, long skies of June. The brindled meadow hides the winding path With interlacing clover, white and red: The blackbirds, startled from their dewy bath, Fly chattering, joyful with imagined dread; The while the whetting scythe foretells the swath, And rings the knell of flowers that are not dead. Now waves of sunlight cross the fields of wheat; The shining crow toward the woodland flies; Far in the fields the larks their notes repeat, And from the fence the whistling partridge cries; Now to the cooling shades the cows retreat, To drowse and dream with mild, half-opening eyes. No other days are like the days in June; They stand upon the summit of the year, Filled up with sweet remembrance of the tune That wooed the fresh spring fields; they have a tear For violets dead; they will engird full soon The sweet full breasts of Summer drawing near. [ Each matchless morning marches from the east In tints inimitable and divine; Each perfect noon sustains the endless feast ' In which the wedded charms of life combine; Sweet Evening waits till golden Day, released, Shall lead her blushing down the world's decline. And when the day is done, a crimson band Lies glowing on the hushed and darkening west; The groups of trees like whispering spirits stand; The robin's song lifts from its trembling breast; The shadows steal out from the twilight land; And all is peace and quietness and rest. —Harper's Magazin.

It was somewhat embarrassing for Aunt Jane when Johnny, a few evenings since at a gathering of friends at his mother's house, asked: " Diciket you know the real Noah, Aunt Jane?" "Pray, sir," said Lady Wallace to David Hume, "I am often asked of what age I am—what answer should I make?" Mr. Hume, immediately guessing her lady- ship's meaning, said, "Madam, when you are asked that question agatn, answer that you are not yet come to years of discretion?' A SOCIAB..E Sell:nue—Once on a time a gentleman liv- ing in St. Louis, an important city in the, United States, used ter spend his evenings in literary work. He had made himself quite comfortable one night in his cosy room before a blazing fire, when he drew his chair up to a table near the wall, and began to write. Presently he was rather taken aback rte seeing a big black spider walk up towards him on the table, quite in a friendly way. The insect showed no fear, but sat looking at the occu- pant of the room with some attention. The gentleman took a straw fmm a broom, and 'moved it gently about the body and legs of the spider, to its great- delight. This lasted ten irunntes, and then, the visitor withdrew. It returned next night, and on every night during winter, when the same performance was gone through, and en- joyed by both parties, but especially by the spider.— Little Folks. . , NERVES ANi) SNAKE Brres.—Noticing in Mr. Robin- son's entertaining " Saunterings in Utah," in the Hm7er's, the statement that snakes cannot jump, calls to mind the massassauga, a species of rattlesnake, hardly as long as one's -arm and nearly as thick, that once infested northern Ohio and other portions of the West of forty years ago. This snake would, according to universal belief,jump to the height of a man's knees, while the bite was generally fatal. The following story illustrates anew the power of the imagination. The writer's grand- father once employed a ' 'hired man," who was exces-1 Lively nervous, and whose existence during harvest time I was embittered by dread'of the massassauga. He ex- -pected an attack at all times; and one day when the field hands had bound their legs to above the knees with bands of straw, as was necessary for protection from the reptiles, and had commenced work, this man sud- denly dropped his scythe, threw up his hands with a ,Ory that he had been bitten and was a dead man, and fainted. He could not be restored to consciousness by ordinary methods, so was carried to the house and put to bed. 'rhe crowd was alarmed, but on looking over, .could find not a bite, neither did any snake appear. The removal of his nether garments disclosed the presence in the seat of his unmentionables of a huge bull-frog! He -was aroused a little, and the " snake" shown him. It ,completed the cure most swiftly. THOTTGRTs AT FolTßScoßE.—Thomas Cooper's "Thoughts at FOUVSCOVe and Earlier" will be welcomed not only by working men—to and about whom he writes so much— but perhaps still more by other classes. Mr. Cooper be- _lieves that the outward circumstances, but not the con- duct, of working men have improved during this cen- tury. "The manners and morals of the working classes —I affirm it on my conscience, and in the teeth of all the boast of our advanced civilisation—were better in England in the early part of this century than they are now. . . . I would much rather witness the shy and simple courtesies of the poor in the old times than the impudence that often takes the name of independence among them now." In his "Sorrowful Thoughts about Strikes," he maintains that it was only the fear of the strength of the laws that kept starving Working men from becoming unruly in 1842. The Lancashire men proved themselves more enlightened during the cotton famine, but the persistent disposition to strike shows that this enlightenment is far from general. In the poli- tical survey, the Liverpool Administration (1812-1827) comes in for a good deal of censure. "The curses of the suffering poor as they mentioned the names of Castle- reagh, and Sidmouth, and Eldon, and Liverpool, seem to ring in my ears yet. • . . . . The wicked Govern- ment sent Oliver, and Castles, and Edwards, their spies, among the poor miserable men, to push them on to overt actions of treason; and Jeremiah Brandreth and -other working men were hung at Derby—and Thistlewood and his associates were hung in London—and there would ' have been nurai hangings had not the strong common sense of Wellington put a stop to these atrocities. Sidmouth has discovered another plot,' said one of the Peers to him one day as they were leaving the House of Lords. am tired of their plots,' was the stern reply, and the Duke set himself to oppose the infamous spy System, and soon brought it to an end, although he con- tinued to support that long, bad Tory Administration of Lord Liverpool. . . . The reckless way in which they sacrificed the interests of England at the peace seems almost incredible if we were not sure that it is a fact. 'What a blockhead was that Lord Castlereagh of yours,' said Napoleon at St. Helena to one of his English Visitors, to sit sprawling his legs under the table at the Congress at Vienna, smirking at the stars and ribbons on his breast—the toys with which the Allies had bam- boozled him—instead of standing up boldly and demand- ing Egypt. It is the real key of your Indian possessions, and you could have had it, or aught else you asked for, 14 the end of the war; Antwerp, for instance, and other Continental ports as depots for your commerce. You had not only given all the strength of your navy and your army to the cause of the allied Soveseigns, but you had subsidised Austria and Prussia and other States with millions upon millions to enable them to carry on the ,war against me and the French people, and nothing would have been denied you.' But that blockheaded and corrupt Ministry asked for nothing, and got nothing as a recompense for our prodigal expenditure of money and human lives." Mr. Cooper finds in war, with its de- struction of men and money, the cause of the distress which periodically, but most surely, afflicts the nations. Were iumours of war to cease the hoarders would feel a return of confidence, and venture anew on trade and commerce in every land. %mai, BOUQUET BLOOM, for beautifying the com- plexion. Heaven is never deaf but when man's heart is dumb. While thy early spring-time is blooming use it: it slips away with no slow foot. It is no help to the sailor to see a flash of light across the dark sea, if he does not instantly steer accordingly.— F. R. HaTergal. The following inscription is on a signboard onthe banks of the Seine, at Billancourt :—" Anglers Rest," and underneath—" Live fish for sale." Brabbit : "Why did you strike my dog? He only smiled at you." Visitor: "Well, captain, you don't ex- pect me to wait till he has had a taste of me, do you?" When the forenoons of life are waked there is not much hope for a peaceful and fruitful evening. Sun. risings and sun-settings are closely connected in every experience. "I have neither time nor inclination to pass paregorics on the deceased," remarked a funeral orator. " Pane- gyrics!" a person present corrected. "As you please, sir,' remarked the orator stiffly; "the words are anony- mous." Go out of doors and get the air. Ah, if you knew what was in the air. See what your robust neighbour who never feared to live in it, has got from it; strength, cheerfulness, power to convince, heartiness and equality to each event. —Emerson. Mistress: "I wish you to do some sweeping to-day" Maid: "To-morrow is my day off, mum, and I never lets myself get tired the day before; because then I can't take no enjoyment when I gets out, mum." "Oh, well do it the day after to-morrow, then." "The day after bein' out I am alters tired, mum." A crusty tenant of an old-fasiiioned Scotch laird pros. sing him to complete some piece of work which had long stood °via., the laird craved further delay, adding that he would give his word of honour, nay, his written bond, to have the thing done before a certain day. "Your word," exclaimed the tenant, "it's weel kenned that will do me little good; and as for your writing, naebody can read it." AsFrench preacher was once descanting from the pul- pit with great eloquence on the beauties of creation. "Whatever," said he, " comes from the hands of Nature is complete; she forms everything perfect." One of his congregation' very much deformed, and having a large hump, went up to him at the close of the discourse and asked, "What think ye of me, holy father—am I per- fect ?" To which the preacher replied, very cooly, " Yes, for a humpbacked man, quite perfect." In a manse in Fife, the conversation of a large party one evening turned on a volume of sermons, which hap just been published with considerable success, and was supposed to have brought a round sum into the hands of the author. When the minister's wife hear of what _ _ _ . . .

had bee-n made by the volume her imagination was ex- cited, and, turning to her husband, wno s .t a little aside, she said, "My dear, I see naething to hind r you to print a few of your sermons, too." "They were a' prin'ed lang syne, said the candid minis er in his wife's ear.

THE PIRATES OF THE CASPIAN.—The Turkoman folk in Central Asia are terrible robbers. They are also slave dealers, selling all the prisoners which they make in war or in their thieving raids. Besides plundering by land, they carry on their evil work by water, for they have a number of pirate ships on the Caspian Sea, which lie in wait for Russian and Persian vessels. They seize all the goods on board these ships, and the unfortunate crews are sold into slavery. The chief markets for slaves are Khiva and Bokhara. Sometimes they have a difficulty in finding purchasers for all their captives if these have been very numerous, and they have been known to dis- pose of a Persian prisoner for a sum equal to eighteen- pence of British money. They keep many slaves to till their fields, and treat them most cruelly.—Little Folks. Somewhat less ancient than most circus jokes is that of a youthful Hebrew, who had been discovered by his horrified parents to have developed a fancy for that succulent dish upon the origin of which the gentle Ella so charmingly descants. The Rabbi was consulted, the suggestion being that the youngster was mad. The holy man dissented from that view, saying that although the action was sinful it w ,s no sign of aberration of intellect. Soon, again, came the parents, this time more alarmed than ever, their son and heir having been discovered performing an osculatory process upon the face of their Gentile handmaid. "Assuredly," they said, he must be mad!" but the priest was still unconvinced. "Son and daughter," he said, "there is certainly much evil in the young man's disposition, but I find no evidence of insanity. If he had kissed the pork and eaten the girl should have thought that he was mad indeed !" WHAT THE SLIM IS MADE OF.—Of the metals dis- covered in the sun, the most important are sodium, magnesium, barium calcium, zinc, copper, aluminium,' nickel, chromium, and iron. Many of the rarer and less- known metals would also appear to be there in some abundance, judging by the facility with which their presence may be detected. Although heavier metals, such as platinum and gold, have not been seen, it by no means follows that they are absent. Their weight would prevent them being easily found by the spectroscope; but it is not outside the bounds of probability that at a future date some enterprising company-mongers may take advantage of scientific discovery, and the gullibility of a small portion of the British public, to offer for sale shares in some imaginary scheme for bringing gold from the sun.—Cassell's Family Magazine. New PAEASOLS.—The new parasols are large, and have curious handles carved with birds and animals, the new shot silk en tout cas, with coloured borders, rejoicing in papier %vile handles, matching in tone and taking the form of very „large rings. Ecru and black parasols are more used than any other, which is fortunate, for they harmonise with all dresses. Ecru muslin parasols with gold ribs are a novelty. If you have by you some semi- worn-out parasols, you may make them a great deal better and fashionable by throwing a canvas handker- chief, with Byzantine bordering edged with lace, across one side, and tacking it on lightly, the so-called hand- kerchief parasol being quite a new idea. Or you may take a wide flounce of Spanish lace and gather it on as full as you can just below the centre point, so that half the lace hangs beyond the parasol all round. There is the Mandarin shape, which is wide and flat, like a Japanese parasol; and the Pagoda raised in the centre after the manner of a pagoda. They are very much trimmed, lace being arranged even on the inside, and full looped bows on the outside. Transparent black parasols are still used, but far more often are lined with a colour such as red, which shows them off better.— Cassell's Family Magazine. THE CIGAR TORPEDO IN THE AMERICAN WAR.—More than one case of conspicuous daring on the part of the Southern naval officers occurred during the war, while using most effectively what is called the cigar torpedo- boat. This was a craft which, when in motion, wa4 entirely immersed, except the top of the funnel, and' might almost be called a submarine torpedo. I remem- ber, on one occasion during the war, when I was at Charleston, meeting in a coffee-room at that place a young naval officer (a Southerner), with whom I got into con- versation. He told me that that night he was going to sink a Northern man-of-war which was blockading the port, and invited me to see him off. I accompanied him down to his cigar-boat, as he called it, and found that she was a vessel about 40 feet long, shaped like a cigar, on the bow of which was placed a torpedo. On his step- ping on board with his crew of four men, his boat was immersed till nothing but a small piece of funnel was visible. He moved off into the darkness at no great speed—say at about five miles an hour. The next even- ing, on visiting the coffee-house, I found my friend sit- ting, quietly smoking his pipe. He told me he had succeeded in making a hole in the frigate which he had attacked, which vessel could, in fact, be seen lying in shallow water some seven miles off, careened over to re- pair damages. But he said that on the concussion made by firing the torpedo, the water had rushed in through the hatches of his boat, and she had sunk to the bottom. All his men were drowned. He said that he didn't know how he escaped himself, but he fancied that he came up through the hatches, as he found kmself floating about. and swam on shore. This affair was officially reported by the American blockading squadron, corroborating the fact of the injury to the frigate, and stating that the torpedo-boat was got up, with four dead bodies in the hold.—Blackwood's Magazine.

TWENTY ONE PEOPLE Bia-rgar NY MAD Doos.—ln Dub- lin, on mind4y, 21 persons were bitten by two mad dogs. Both were killed by the police after an exciting chase. The first doz passed along the southern part of the city as the people were pouring out of the different churches. While passing through Jamea-street and Thomas-street seven per- sons were attacked and bitten, all of whom were attended to in Sreeven's Hospital. The total number reported to have been bitten by this dog was 18. Reaching Meath-street the brute seized a little boy named Shiel, and it was while hold- ing on to the poor child that the constables succeeded in battering its skull with their truncheons. Similar scenes were enacted at the north side of the city. About twelve o'clock cors,ernation was caused in Monntjoy-street by a large rabid bull-terrier biting at every one it passed. A man named Fagan was severely bitten on both legs, and had to be at once conveyed to the hospital. The animal after- wards turned into Paradise-place, where it attacked and worried a goat to death. Passing through Frederick-street it attacked a boy named William Rooney and bit him on the race and right leg. In Capel-street the animal bit in two places on the left leg William White, Finally it sought refuge in the area of a house in Jervis-street, where it was shot. ESTABLISHED NEARLY 50 YEARS. ' The average proportion of cheese from inilk is usually understood to be 11b. of cheese to the gallon of milk, that is to 101bs. of milk. In New Zealand, the Waiko factory .state definitely that they have made 15ozs. to the 101bs. Ternuka Eas made 1740z5. from 111bs. Edendale pro- duced 125,408 gallons of milk and made 129,2551b5. of marketable cheese, a clear gain of 3,2031b5. of cheese over gallons of milk. .

Tri'i WELSH Lawson; SEASON.—kccounts of the lamb- ! ing season from various parts of North Wales show that the present season is one of the best on record. The ' weather has been less severe and disastrous than has been known for some years past, and the results of the season on the hills are exceptionally good. The snow- fall has been lighter than usual, and there has conse- quently been no scarcity of grass. SWEET ENSILAGE.—Mr. George Fry, F.L.S., has just issued a small and interesting book on Sweet Ensilage. i The greater part of the matter has already appeared n articles written for the agricultural journals, but it has now been arranged in interesting form. Mr. Fry has devoted considerable study and labour in conducting his experiments, and has divided his remarks into two parts—(l) Theoretical, which may be supposed to be addressed to scientific agriculturists; and (2) Practical, which will no doubt be Of great use to practical farmers. THE Scowl( SHEEP TRADE.—During the last few weeks numerous important sheep stock valuations and sales have taken place in the South of Scotland. Both valua- tions and sales have been marked by very heavy de- creases in prices compared with last year, so far as Cheviot and cross sheep are concerned, the valuation rates being 10 to 20 per cent. lower, while the forced sale rates were 20 to nearly 40 'per cent. lower. On the other hand, black-faced sheep pf out-standing merit have in- creased in value from sto nearly 10 per cent. Shrop- shire sheep have about maintained their prices. PROFESSOR SHELDON'S CANDIDATURE.—The Derbyshire farmers, after making a great fuss about sending one of their own class to Parliament, and selecting Professor Sheldon, have caved in, through party prejudice. Many of them refuse to support Mr. Sheldon because he is a Liberal. One enlightened individual, a land agent, understood that the proposed candidate had once taken the chair for Joseph Arch (a mistake, as it happens), and that is enough for him, poor creature. Mr. Sheldon will find no difficulty in obtaining the support of a more enlightened constituency, and the Derbyshire farmers will probably have some nominee of the landlords to re- present them. THE NUTRITIVE POWER OF Oters.—Herr Kalif, a Ger- man agricultural authority„ affirms that the nutritive power of oats is considerably augmented by steeping the grain in water before giving it to horses. This is his plan. He has three troughs, each of which holds as much oats as will be required for one day's feeding. The first day the first trough is filled with corn and water at ' a temperature of 8 deg. (centigrade) poured over it, and the whole mass is well stirred; the water is left.in the trough about six hours, after which it is strained off through a hole in the bottom of the trough: The next day the operation is repeated in the second trough, and again on the following day the third trough. The oats thus steeped get up fermentation, and at the expiration of about forty-eight hours it is ready to be given to the horses, and will then, according to Herr Kalif, produce its maximum nutritive effect. This admitted or better demonstrated by actual experiments, it follows as a natural corollary that the amount of. corn may be diminished and a saving effected, which it may be in- ferred would more than counterbalance the expense of heating the required amount of water, and the slight additional labour involved in the treatment suggested.

HEREFORD CATTLE AT LORGRIDGE.—The following testimony to the progress of the Hereford breed of cattle, outside the district proper from which it takes its name, is from Lad Gillespie, who writes to the Hereford Times as follows :--" I see that Mr. T. Kay, of Longridge, Preston, is among the purchaser of Hereford cattle. I wish him success. Hitherto, I bent ve, I have been the only Lancashira member of the Hereford Herd Book Society, but more as an admirer than as a breeder, my accommodatim being limited. Still, I have kept a few white-face during the six years I have been resi- dent in this county, ,and, I am pleased to my, have always done well. The Herefords are, without doubt, gradually creeping northwards. Within a short dis- tance of here there are six graziers, and, I understand, another lot further north. Some years ago about 20 grazed, and two of the Preston butchers, who killed part of them, informed me that they were much pleased with them. I have also sold several in the neighbourhocri for slaughter, and these have in general given satisfaction. Frequently the stigma is cast up-az Herefords as to being poor dairy cattle. No doubt, as a rule, as to quan- tity of ml k, they are deficient, in comparison with some other breeds; but I thinlr the richness of quality will quite compensate for the deficiency. Of this I feel cer- tain, that were the Herefords only given a fair trial along with other breeds as to general usefulness (easily kept, hardiness of constitution, &c.), we should soon -ee a much greater spread of the white-faces in our English home counties." Ho r WEATHER AND WASTE IN THE DAIRY.—One of the most important things that a butter-making farmer ' should consider at the present moment is hoc' to prevent the tremendous waste which he is almost invariably accustomed to submit to during the hot months of summer. ' Milk is greatly affected by temperature, and it frequently happens that it becomes sour within 12 hours, in which case it is unfit for consumption, or it is considered so, which in this country is almost the same thing, and is given away to pigs before the whole of the cream has risen. Thus it is that when the cows are yielding their best upon grass there is a periodical loss of a large per centage of butter which their milk contains. Producers have frequently been urged to adopt some method to prevent this, but they seldom take any notice of advice upon the point, and I question if they do not think that such advice is absolutely worthless. If, as in the case of cheese made from skim milk, they were shown the solid material which had been abstracted from it, they would perhaps consider the matter worthy of attention. I can recommend no better plan for adoption than the following :—A given quantityof milk, saylllolb., equivalent to about 10 gallons, is divided into two equal portions during very hot weather. One portion should be set in open pans in the dairy, skimmed in the ordi- nary way, the cream churned, and the butter carefully weighed. The other portion should be put into a deep can—say 2ft. in depth, with a width,of 20in. by 91n., for example. This can of milk, without a lid, is to be placed in a vessel of very cold water at a temperature of about 45 degrees Fahrenheit, and allowed to stand for 12 hours. At the end of this period the cream should be taken off the milk and permitted to stand until it has soured,when it should be churned and weighed. It will then be found that the butter is considerably larger in bulk or weight, and equal in quality, if not superior, to that made from the other cream. An experiment like this would be a sufficiently tangible proof one way or the other, and the farmer could instantly calculate how many pounds of butter he is weekly losing by not following up the vari- ous systems of dairying which are now popular. This, however, is not all, for the loss in the skimmed milk and buttermilk is almost as great as the loss of butter. Sour skim milk is of of no use except for swine. At all events , farmers in this country will not use it, although French farmers are fond of it for their calves; but as the whole of the cream is raised in 12 hours when it is placed in cold water as indicated, the skim-milk is perfectly sweet and fit for sale or conversion into cheese. DEVON CATTLE.—In America, Devons are not yet ex- tensively known, but where they are soon find favour. An old breeder writes—" If I were young again, I would go on with the same cattle. It I had the grass of Ken- tucky, I would keep Devons for grazing, for they carry more high-priced meat to the shambles, take flesh faker, make as much butter, and are morelhardy for any sec- tion than any breed I know of." Stanley Griswold, who founded his herd thirty-four years ago, usually keeps about forty head, and thinks the Devons the best for milk and 'butter of any that he has had, having tested them with Durhams, Ayrshires, and Jerseys, and finds none that makes such good butter and pay so well for their feed. They are hardy, keep easily, make the best beef, and for the yoke are not excelled by any breed. C. H. Jewell says—" The Devons are the most hardy, easiest to keep, and make a better quality of beef and more of 'it, according to the amount of food consumed, make the best draught cattle, being easier to train and quicker of motion than any other breed." J. A. Pomery, after speaking of the popularity of other breeds in the dairies of his neighbourhood, adds—" But we make as much 'butter from a cow as the best of them. We average 230 pounds per annum to the cow in a dairy of 24 cows." Another breeder says—" As to feed and care, I can raise three Devons on less feed and with less care than I can two Shorthorns, and the three will make more and better beef than the two Shorthorns; and, being hardier than the Shorthorns, the losses in calving by accident and want of care is much less." As to Devons under the butter test, Dr. Cheston Morris, a recognised authority in America, says—" For some fifteen years I made butter, and my yearly average varied from 170 lb. to 175 lb. per cow. As compared with other stock, the Devons in our section require less care, are more hardy and thrive on less food than any other breed, though with them, as with others, good feeding, not pampering,lpays. As milkers, when the quality of the milk is considered, they I are second to none. For several years I have been in the habit of placing at the agricultural shows, side by side in a box with ice, jars filled with milk obtained from the cows of the different breeds on exhibition, such as Jersey, Guernsey, Ayrshire, and Shorthorn. The cream line stood nearly equal in the two first-named with the Devon, perhaps sometimes one-eighth of an inch more, but was much less in the latter—Ayrshire and Short- horn. The skim-milk was poorest in the Jersey, and successively richer in the rest, but could not 'compare with the Devon. I think that the great richness of the
Devon milk causes it to part with its cream more slowly, and hence has arisen the erroneous impression that they are not butter cows."

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

Lars Pass.—Now is a good time to sow these to come in for exhibition about the end of August, though a week or ten days may be gained or lost according to the season. The safest plan is te, make two sowings with that interval, and one is sure to be right for the time stated. If the ground is dry at the time of sowing the first lot they should be soaked in water for twelve hours and the channels or drills watered • also, and the seeds covered mat once. This will make a difference of a week any time to seeds coming up. So it is evident ' that if the first lot were sown in the usual way during dry weather and the next during moist they would differ but little from one sowing. Some make a trench as for Celery for these late sowings of Peas, and fill it with manure and soil in equal portions. Any spare Emit is arranged on each side to be used as a mulching forth Peas, as well as to fill up the trench when its contents have shrunk, which they generally do by the time. th( Peas are a foot or two high. No more soil should be placed to them than will bring the trench to the ground level, as it would interfere with the waterijig of the plants if raised higher. It is obvfous that the object of this method is to place as much food as possible within the immediate reach of the root, and by constant water- ing in dry weather with either manure or clear water they are induced to remain within the boundary of the trench. On light or sandy soil the above method of dealing with late Peas is the best that can be devised. The plan generally adopted on other soils is to draw a drill four to six inches deep and about three inches wide and scatter the seed thinly in these. If the ground is moderately loose on each side of the row the roots will spread some distance, and in ordinary seasons will scarcely require any. water. Some growers make a broad but equally shallow channel to sow the seeds, and when they are up the rows look as if they were quite one foot across. This may answer very well providing no more seeds are deposited than in a space half the width, otherwise they cannot fail to overcrowd each other. We would advise our readers to mix red lead with the seeds in the way previously described in this column. When we made our last sowing this was omit- ted, as we could see no traces of mice about the garden. But in less than a week they were busy burrowing into the rows and would soon have destroyed them. Having an excellent cat on the premises, we carried it to the Pea rows late at night, having first deposited some scraps of bloaters and a dead bird or two.. We now find pussy paying frequent visits to the rows of Peas, and it is needless to say there has been no further mischief wrought by the mace. The sorts usually sown for ex- hibition purposes are Telegraph, Telephone, Criterion, and Omega. Crops of Peas in an advanced stage should have supports placed to them before they fall over. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Carnations are sufficiently ad- vanced to have stakes placed to them to support the flower stems, and where these are numerous and thickly placed they may be shown to greater advantage If the sticks are inserted obliquely, instead of upright. We sometimes see sticks quite half an inch in diameter used for this purpose, when some half that thickness would suffice for what there is to carry. If a few dozen red deal stakes, painted green are annually used thy become expensive on account of the portion buried in the ground decaying, so as not to be safe for another year. If pieces of painted wire are used, cut the desired `length, they will last an age. If shorter pieces, about a foot long, have their stakes attached to them with wire bound round a few times, they will also answer the pur- pose. Arum Lev, if still in pots,. may be planted in rich soil, which may be prepared by taking a spadeful or two of soil out and introducing some good manure into the hole, mixed with some soiL Each plant should have a stout itake placed firmly into the soil, and a piece of string tied round it and then loosely round the leaves of the plant. If kept. well watered during dry weather they will makegrowth as thick as an ordinary wrist and throw up large spathes at the proper time. Deutzias, Dielytras and Spireas are best planted out after this time. The latter may be, indeed must be, divided into two or three pieces if they are to occupy a similar sized pot next season. The soil must be firmly pressed round each plant, and the crowns should be rather below than above the level of the soil. THE WINDOW.—Boxes for outside the window are planted in various ways, and geraniums always occupy the greater portion of space, as the limited area allowed for the roots is conducive to a floriferous condition. They may form a row at the side nearest the window, and may be mixed or all of one colour, and none is so effective as a good scarlet, such as Vesuvius or Star of Fire. The front or the side furthest from the window may ' have a plant or two of the Variegated Grass (Dactylis Glomerate), which is a perfectly hardy plant. Intermixed with this, Blue Lobelia looks very well. If an odd plant or two of Troixeolum Canariensis (Canary Creeper) are put in they may be trained to cover the front of the boxes. One of the common Tropreolum at each end of the box, and trebled each side the window, looks remarkably...pretty.

But when the digestive organs are impaired the food taken Into the stomach becomes sour and fermented, followedlby decay and putrefac- tion. The result is the formation of a poisonous acrid secretion that causes a faint distressed sensation attended with head- ache. This acrid secretion is taken into the circulation, and the b ood bee Ailing thus poisoned permeates the whole system, carrying the poison wherever it goes. This produces a weak languid feeling which makes life miserable. After a time pimples, blotches, bolls, and sores break out on the skin, which is NATE RE'd CRY FOR HELP to be relieved of this poison, a simple matter if we adopt the proper measures. div.head: FAIR CANOEIST.
div.p: A FAIR CANOEIST.

"Eagy, Jim, let go!" says the stalwartcilef boatman of H.M. coastguard-statiox at Bridlington Quay to his mate, as they lovrer the aytie down from their shoulders on to the yellow rand, where 01 long rollers break in lines of sparkling foam. "I am afraid, mies, you will get a bit of a wetting going through there," he adds, nodding towards the waves, as he tucks the macintosh apron carefully rotted the well combing of the canoe, and over the white flannel dress of Skipper Adeline. -
"Ol;,I can manage them, Barker. Thanks. All righl— Pus.".ffl"

- A vigorous heave; and the little ship is afloat and the pad-1 dle dips readily, whilte the two coastguards-men stand to, watch how she will ride through the broken water and good-- humouredly look for a white curling surf to breab suddenly over the sharp bows. Bet the tayre pilot is a right skilful one—a pair of bright eyes see each comber as it ruihes shoreward, and nimble firm little hands wield the paddle consummately.

"Back a couple of strokes "—"Easy !"—" Go aNtad!" prt-hand "—" Easy- starboard!" The blue-mono- gramed blades flash and dip, now slow/y—now vigorously, and the wee barkie glides down across the back of the last wavelet, having shipped never a thimbleful, and than lios-to in smooth water, waiting for her consort the Vol3ung to-put off and join her. . . .

But although a member of the Rhyat Canoe Club, and a voyager of much experience on waters. both :salt and fresh, the *Litany's skipper runs thesurf in a lobberly fashion, and in his haste rashly "rushes " the little- breakers instead of coolly dodging them, and pays the penalty thereof by getting a lot of sparkling water inboard. But the sponge, which is the little craft's pump, soon makes matters com- fortable, and then stretchers are got right, back-boards fixed, and sleeves rolled up "Are you ready?" "Aye, aye, sir!" " Paddle ! " And the tiny fleet forges merrily through the green waters on I a course laid for Flanebro' Head, which stands, almost hid- ' den oma summer haze. The strains of a lively waltz come floating from the sea-wall parade, and the stone piers of the harbour begin to shimmer in the heat as the boats voyage onward. Now the cliffs begin to show a rich brown, fringed along the base by white pebble ridges with, golden corn. fields a-top. Beyond is a fine view of the town of Bridling- ton—"old Bollington," as the natives call it—looking very quaint and picturesque with red-tiled roofs, and its grand Ptdory Church" standing like a sentinel on guard, recalling bygone days when its priors were 101-d of life and limb,, and the famed "St. John of Bridlington" flourished.

A good tide is still running, for it wants yet an hour to low water, and the canoes have made a quick run and are off Sewerby Cliffs, where the village looks a veritable pic- ture in the warm sunlight, and the Hall peeps out grey and stately from amongst its sheltering woods. Below these cliffs a grim sea-fight took place long ago between Paul Jones, the daring Yankee pirate so called, and two of the king's ships, in which the English came off badly, to the dismay of the country folk who watched the battle from the cliff-top, for the moon was at the full and lighting up _ _

" Clytie ahoy! Steer for Dana's Dyke !" And in ten minutes' time the boats are rocking no opposite the opening of a gorse.clad ravine running nu from the beach; a long mound skirts the crest of it to eastward, and this, so antiquarians hold, is an earthwork of the early Britons, forming part of a great svatem towards Malian. Tradition has named it after the Danes, and very likely, if not origi- nally thrown np, yet it was used by the men who landed with Ida at Flamboro' when he came to win the kingdom of Northumbria.

But the tide which "waits for no man" bears the squadron onward, under the shadow of the rugged cliffs, which are daszling white in the noontide glare— for the chalk has taken the place of clay—on past a' projecting point into the shallow little bay which forms the "Routh Landing" of Flamboro'. To the left Is the Lifeboat House, and through the open doors the lofty blue and white bows of the Matthew Middle. Wood peep out, one of the fine trim boats belonging to the Royal National Lifeboat Institution. A group of gaudily-painted cobbles are drawn up on the slope which leads fro,n the shore, backed by the dusty road to the village some mile or 80 inland. It is a pretty little bit of coast scenery, with a few women painting the boats, and here and there a sedate donkey nibbling the herbage on the grassy steeps, giving a touch of life to the whole.

w—ave Crom the blne-petticoated women ashore who shout some shrill greeting, and a bend' in the chalk wall shuts in the bay. A long surface of brown seaweed- covered rocks lies between the ebbing water and the cliff- foot, and the waves laugh and dance amongst them with a hissing rise and fall. Paddling is right hungry work, so the corn- modore signals his fleet to follow, as the Volsung, very carefully steering between two black points, shoots into a perfect little harbour formed by a curving ledge of rock which rises some two feet above the water. Having landed, the crews haul the canoes well up on a patch of ribbed sand, and then unlading the provisions from the lockers, stagger over fifty yards, and after countless slips and plashings into tiny. pools, reach the belt of boulders which line the cliff- foot, and then all hands are piped to dinner. The sun is shining warm and bright over a sea which mirrors the cloud- less blue of the sky, a soft breeze just ruffles the water, and a pair of kittiwakes are circling round, whilst the silence is broken by the musical murmur of the summer sea. Ab ! the utter bliss of basking on such a day in the ease of flannels and lazily thinking of nothing at all, knowing that there is no one to trouble, and that you half-dreamily can let the minutes fly unheeded ! Can you though? Not with a flowing tide and unmoored boats. The look-out-man, sleepily casting a glance seawards, reuses at once to action —the canoes are rocking and softly bumping as the ripples creep up ,fast—" All hands aboard !" The Volsung's crew rushee recklessly down over the treacherous ground in wild haste, leaving the Clpties captain to gather up the stores and come more leisurely and safely, and by the time she has reached the water's edge the little ships are floated off. But now comes a difficulty—one of those slight occurrences which add to the charm and vary the day's work in canoe- ing. The rock on which the landing was effec'ed is now at least eighteen inches covered, and instead of riding quietly in the little habonr which it formed, the barkies are tossing and rolling on the surges which come splashing over it, and to reach them their crews must get through the shallow water on the shore. The Volsung's pilot, used to such trifles, plunges boldly with the stores to each and then re- turns, and before the ell.tie's crew can mutiny, catches her in his arms and splashes out to sea with her laughing lady- ship. A spirit of mischief seizes the Yolsung, for as the pant- ing boatman nears it, away it drifts on the bashwash out of reach. A false step and he is off the rock and waist-deep,' but (how, he never knew) regains it; and there behold him balancing fearfully on one leg, and with the other foot making frantic efforts to catch the saucy craft, holding all the while no feather-weight in his arms, whilst a merry voice rings in his ears' threatening dire punishments—" You let me drop if you dare, sir !" A stagger, a plunge! and somehow the little lady is safely aboard, and Ole half- drenched voyager is free to capture and climb into his own Canoe.

" What is that speck out there, 770/sung 2" "Snaithic Sand North Buoy," answers the pilot. " Let us paddle round it t" and so the stems are pointed away from the land, and work begins steadily again. The Yoleung's cibin-boy laughs softly to himself as he remembers the tide is flowing strongly; and the much-enduring skipper, whose arms still feel the effects of the late embarkation, feels a glow of fiendish joy to think how his fair fellow- voyager will have to ply paddle mightily if ever the Clytie is to round that buoy. A quarter-hour's pull and the struggle begins, for the pair are fairly in the tideway, and the little ships make very slow head against it; but there is no thought of giving up aboard either, and at last the great red and white-ringed iron boiler-like structure is alongside, and the sailing-masters can read the words "North Smithic," and see the waters foam and rash pass as though they would tear it from its moorings twenty feet below.
"What about the Held—can your do it?" signals the commodore.

"Of course I can," comes the ;indignant hail from the fayre skipper. "Then full speed ; we have no time to spare." As the boats draw nearer to the famous headland, the gentle motion of the bay-swell begins to grow into the long lifting of the rollers as they come in from the open sea, for the fleet is rocking now on deep waters, and white horses are showing around, whilst from the beach, some half-a-mile on the port beam, comes thn muttered thunder of the surf which is breaking in long white patchei on the shore There is grand old Flamboro' Head, with its splen- did lighthouse, showing a column of shapely whiteness against the sky, from which at sundown a bright red light will show, and then die down and change to a point of yellow, which too grows and grows and then fades feebly, until it brightens up oace more, to fade again and change into a red.
Twn whtfee t, one rout Indicate!' Flamb ro' Head. says the pilot-book.

-The rugged wall of chalk standing boldly against the heaving might of the wild North Sea, with its scarred face pierced by dusky hollows and dark mysterious caverns, is always a glorious study, but to-day there is a sight out be- yond not to be forgotten. A large four-masted ship with all sail set, stun'-sails alow and aloft, glistening spotless in the sun, is majestically gliding southward, her long low hull, painted black and white, showing the foaming seas piling up before her cut-water and then rushing aft and bubbling away under the counter in a seething track be- hind. There is an " overfall " just off the Head—foul ground this is, where the water is always lumpy, however fine the day and smooth the sea, and the canoes toss and plunge braatly, burying their decks under sparkling foam. No place this for a novice to try and navigate, but the Vol- sung's skipper has often sailed her here, and the CkSie's captain is a fearless and ready canoeist, and so through the turmoil they steer, heedless of the dash and splash of chop- ping seas, until the bay opens north of the point, and Flam- boro' Head is rounded.

"Too much swell on to try the caves," pronounces the pilot, " and it's going to blow up wet, so 'bout ship It is rather a ticklish bit of work to run a Rob Roy in the midst of a cross-sea, for it is a dangerous thing to get broad- side on to waves if somewhat big, yet the aytie is spun round so nimbly that the commodore is provoked to shout "Well done, indeed!" as he leads the way homewards. The Srnithic Buoy drops astern once more, the sea grows smoother, and a long roll takes the place of the tossing waves, over which the ships ride merrily with an easy motion. Half-a-mile south of the head there are several de- pressions in the cliff, sending wondrous echoes back over the sea if you call to them, and standing in to try, the Vol- sung's pilot grows careless, and, forgetful of the swell sowing

in, lets his vestal drift broadside close to the beach. Sad- denly there is a hiss and, without a moment's warning, the monad of water Cods over and comes sweeping in, in a wall of foam. With a ample of frantic strokes on the starboard hand the canoe is just eased up to meet it, and then it breaks, a deluge of cold water over the bows, and dashes up to the waist of the crew,. half filling the well and all but capsizing the little craft, and it takes all that the skipper knows to prevent her beg washed broadside on to the beach. Thoroughly ashamed of himeslf he loos eagerly round, hoping his fellow-voyager, has not noted the stupid performance, but derisive lauNater rippling across the water tells him the hope is vain, and for long after that day a certain talent was ever keenly felt. Homeward in the quiet evenetie across the calm bosom of the bay, with the sun sinking behind the Boynton Woods and iihshina the western sky a rosy crimson, whilst the gentle land breeze brings now and again the tuneful voices cf the priory bells. . .
As the pla-rs of—Bridlington rise Prom the gray sea ad nearer, both trews pall themselves to3ether to rua into har- bour in their very best form.

Half a dozesi-v.oltin—te;s—p.romotly seize the canoes and carry them urrinto the boat-house, and,as the coastguards- man on duty lakes charge of them and wishes "Good night," he adds, l• Yon have done a rare good day's work, miss, and I guess you are the first lady who has been round Flatubro' Head in a•canoe."—From Casse3l's Jfagazine for June.

div.head: ' THREE DAYS IN SCOTLAND. BY J. D.
div.p: ' THREE DAYS IN SCOTLAND. BY J. D.

--- • - • The imrressions 'lft upon my mind after my fiat vitit to Scotland are of a truly delight%l character, and vivid remembrances of the few happy hours I spent in the • Highlands and among the Lochs oft that country will be w lifelong sense of the keenest gratification. To one, like myself, accustomed to the never varying" scenery" of tall smoky chim-- neys, crowded streets, dirty slums" and alleys, the change to the mountainous country and pieturesque lakes nestling among,thir hills of "Bonnie Scotland" ia indeed, one never to.be forgotten. Though my stay. among the mountain-lochs of North Britain was only.brief, yet I had opportunities, of which I availed myself, of. observing their majestic gran- deur, and of confirming the truth of its designation as "The land of mountain and of flood," With promontory, creek, and bay. And inauutains that like g aats stand To sentinel enchanted land. When sailing upon the clear waters ot pretty. En- glish lakes among the hills of Cumberland and driving along some of the mountain passes of that district, or enjoying visits to.the principal places of interest in and near London, Liverpool, or Man- chester, I felt proud, as am Englishman, of the country which gave me birth,.but the most pleasur- able sensations of my life have been aroused by my visit to the land of the Wallaces and Bruces, the Macgregors and the Campbells. One of the plea- santest features of rgy trip .was. a friend, who well knew the country, understood the manners and Customs of the people, and. what was equally im- portant, naturally acquainted with the broad Scotch dialect. At an early, hour on the • morning of Whit-Mon- day, comfortably seated in one of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company's car- riages, we were being rapidly driven towards the North of England, when, after passing Lancaster and its famous castle, we • had, through the misty atmosphere,. a glimpse of More- cambe Bay—our last view of Lancashire. After a stoppage of forty minutes at Oxenholme Junction the journey was resumed, and. Carlisle was reached shortly after five o'clock. Here our comfort was slightly interfered with by a Scotch family of eight persons entering the carriage, which had previously found accommodation for four human beings. One of the sons was securing the tickets at the booking office, and we were afforded considerable amusement by the cries of the father " Willum, whaur's ta tickets?" to which the mother replied with the earnest entreaty "Sit ye doon, .ronn, and dinna pit yersel aboot." After the anxiety. of the worthy sire had been relieved by the appearance of " Willum," the train again started, and we drew up in Eglinton- street Station, Glasgow, shortly after eight o'clock. Here we alighted, but other excursionists proceeded onward to the Central Station. My , first day, was ;Tent in Glasgow and its suburbs, and in observing its general features . and characteristics, I cannot do More, in this brief notice, than merely allude to Glasgow—the com- mercial metropolis of Scotland, and the most popu- lous town across the Border." The manufactures of Glasgow are chiefly cotton goods; but shipbuild- ing, and the coal and iron trades. have of recent years been largely developed. Its principal thorough- fares are well laid out, with elegant business pre- raises after the style of those in the West End of London and the fashionable quarters of Manchester and Liverpool. The custom of living in fiats at Glasgow was the most striking novelty to me, as a "Lancashire lad." The fiat system certainly pos- sesses many conveniences, but L still prefer the good old Lancashire custom of every man' S house being considered his castle. But more than every- thing else were the courtesy, kindness, and respect with which I was treated. The friend who accompanied me, or rather whom I accompanied, took me along the principal streets and through the West End of the city, with its many fashionable terraces and crescents—the residences of the local aristocracy. We next entered the West End Park, comprising the 'highly picturesque lands of Wood- lands and Kelvin Grove, purchased by the Corpora- tion at a cost of nearly £lOO,OOO. were we had a splendid view of the University of Glasgow, a mag- nificent building in which over way it is looked at. It is surmounted by a central tower 300 feet in height. The : foundation stone was laid by the Prince and Princess of Wales in 1868, and the open- ing ceremonial took place in 1870.. We next pro- ceeded through Kelvin Grove Museum, and on our way "home' I was shown most of the principal public and private buildings, banks, &c., in the city, crossed the riVer Clyde near the Broomielaw, or harbour of Glasgow, with its vessels of every description and size; and had pointed out to me the many monuments perpetuating the memory of some of Scotland's and Britain's heroes. The day's ramble, coupled with the long railway journey to Glasgow in the early morning, induced sound sleep, and it is needless to add that on the following morning I felt very much refreshed. Seven o'clock. on Tuesday morning saw us on board the fine new steamship "Grenadier" bound to Ardrishaig and back, a sail of over 180 miles. The "Grenadier" is a splendidly-fitted up vessel, and had been sailing only from the previous Wednesday. There is every,convenience provided for the comfort and pleasure of excursionists, one interesting feature being the excellent meals in. the dining saloon. During our sail we partook of breakfast, dinner, and tea on board, and certainly L never enjoyed better meals, and no one could have. desired them to be more courteously served. The weather was beauti- fully fine, and our sail down the Clyde was most en- joyable. Each bank was lined with vessels, chief among which were well known American liners, such as." Hibernia," " " Devonia," "Ethio- pia," "Roumania," &c. As we sailed along we passed numberless shipbuilding establishments, and above the bustle and noise on board the " Grena- dier " could be heard the merry rattle of the ham, mers of the workmen. In passing, it may be stated that so rapid has been the progress of shipbuilding on the Clyde that at the. present time it exceeds that of all the other parts of Great Britain combined. Undoubtedly much of its progress has been promoted by the extensive widening and deepening operations which have been effected in the bed of the river, and in the " Grenadier " we passed several steam dredges at work along the channel. Greenock was our first principal calling place, though before reaching here the river had widened considerably, and assumed the appearance of an: im- mense lake. We had passed Dunglass Castle with an Obelisk to the memory of Henry Bell, the origina- tor of steam navigation in Europe; and Dumbarton Castle, which figures prominently amidst the beauti- ful scenery on a rock of considerable height, stand- ing out into the river. Greenock is an important town on the bank of the Clyde, and the, harbours and 'docks are almost continually thronged with vessels trading to all parts of the world. After a passing glance at Port Matilda, with its seven guns, on Bat- tery Point, we were interested by the magnificent and changing scenery. There was a brief stoppage at Dunoon, one of the oldest and most important watering places on the West Coast, and after cross- ing the channel we arrived at charmingly situated Rothesay, the county town of Bute. A few minutes later, while crossing Rothesay Bay, I was astonished, on being addressed by an apparent strang. "Are yOu from B—?' mentioning a populous Lancashire town. "Well," replied I"I am not from B , but I have been at B—." My in- terrogator continued, "Did you ever attend the school in G—street, B— l'" I confessed that such was the fact—a confession which brought back memories of my boyhood. Other questions and ex- planations followed, and I was agreeably surprised to find, by an accidental meeting, that I was speak- ing to one of my old school mates, whom I had not seen for over 13 years. By the vicissitudes of life he had left B— for Lincolnshire many years ago, and he, too, WAS Qll a brief visit to Scotland, He, like my-

An the dreadful consequences the right hon. baronet bad predic.ed—the cessation of barley growing and the adultera- tion of,beer—was to be caused by increasing the duty from 20 10 23 per cent. (Laughter.) After making this unwise proposal the right hon. baronet suggested a larger duty on wine. (Opposition cheers.) The right hon. baronet recom- mended an increase of the wine duty, as being specially in- jurious to Spain. He desired to point out that any propo- sal specially injurious to the trade of Spain would be in- jurious and perhaps fatal to the small but growing trade with the British Colonies—(Ministerial cheers)—including Free-trade colonies like New South Wales. The proposal to impose preferential duties was impracticable. If he defeated the Government he must take the responsibility of that de- feat, and be prepared to go forward with his proposals for the taxation of tea and have the courage of his opinions. The Government had had the courage of their opinions. This was not altogether a popular Budget, but it would be a very popular Budget in ComparllNl With the rival Budget of the right hon. gentleman. (Ministerial cheers.) This amendneent could not be considered as a mere question of a change ill the Budget. It Was a question of life or cleat' and it wenald be far the tight hon. gentleman if he dere them on this occasion to try if he could form a Gove.,Gule'_. to carry out the policy he had placed before the, e,ountry,": Those who eat On his aide of the House Ea:llia singularly elated with the right hen, gentleman'elSpee'lm. They could not hado A better cry to go before the Country with. The time would COEIB when the Tory party would Tegret having proposed a duty on tea, and having sneered at the temper- ance party in thia hountry. (Minieterialltheere.) Lord OROROB liamtrzoo: said the right hon. gentleman was good enough at the beginning df tis speech to denounce clap-trap, whereas towards the close of it he had indulged in a good deal of it (Opposition cheers.) In conclusion he commented at length on the proposals in the Budget to Sus- pend the repayment of the debt.—Mr. O'Surravaor, in an animated speech, maintained that the proposed increase of the spirit duty would have the effect of relieving taxation in England at the expense of taxpayers in Scotland and Ire- laud..—Mr. O'Beirne, Mr. C. S. Read, and Mr. Coops joined he the discussion; and Dr. CAMERON, who strongly objected to an increase in the day on whisky, contended that taxa- tion should 'fall equally upon the different sections of the community, which, as regards the duty on alcohol, might be attained by imposing a duty of 40 to 6cl on every gallon of proof spitit'in either beer, wine, or whisky.—Mt. ARNOLD contended that there was a decided unreality in the amend- ment, which, he maintained, was in effect playing the working man argument for the advantage of the wealthier classes.—Mr. Oen EWING dwelt on the injustice to the agricultural interest which would be caused by the increase in the spirit duties, and on its demoralising effect its stimu- lating adulteration.—Mr. WHITBREAD eriticieed the pro- posed increase of the beer duties, especially if they were to I be permanent.—Mr. A. O'CONNOR referred to the returns illustrating the falling off in various British industries and the increase in foreign trade, contending that the Budget would strike a blow at home industry white benefiting the foreign p-oducer. Mr. CHILDERS said an increased duty generally led to a falling off in consumption, and that had been fully consi- fiered in his estimate of the result of increasing the duty on spirits and beer. At the first view he thought the ob- jection contained in the amendment was that there was no increased duty on wine corresponding to that on spirits, but he was surprised to hear from Sir M. Hicks-Beach that what was objected to was the increased duty on spirits. He maintained that increased duties on liquors were preferable to increased duties on tea or longer. He contended that spirits and beer were the most suitable articles of consump- tion to bear increased taxation.

Sir S. Noramccrrn agreed with Dr. Cameron that the question before the House should be treated as a fiscal one. He was not satisfied with the explanation of the Govern- ment as to the 'fiscal ground on which beer and spirits were selected. Sir M. Hicks-Beach merely mentioned the tea duty as an illustration of his argument, and his argument was fastened upon by Sir C. Dilke to raise a false issue. The Government's object was to produce the impression that they were forwarding the cause of temperance. The Government said people should be burdened in order to re- strain their desire to go to war, but it was the Government, not the people, that went into warlike enterprises. On the whole they ought to keep as far as possible the taxation of the country steady. He was in favour when necessary of raising a large sum of money by terminable annuities spread over a few years, so as to steady the burden of the taxpayer. _ . _

Mr. Ortantrotendeclared that there was a very moderate degree of connection between the speech of Sir S. Northcote and the view on which the judgment of the House was in- vited. Comparing the financial arrangements of the late Government with those of the present, Mr. Gladstone showed that Sir Stafford Northcote had taken office with a surplus of six millions, and that his habitual finance was one of annual deficit, whereas for four years the present Government had paid the expenses of the country out of revenue, and had exhibited a surplus the present year, a deficit being quite exceptional. As to the motion of Sir Michael Hicks Beach, he declared it to be one aimed at the life of the Government. While hon. gentlemen opposite complimented his right hon. friend on recognising the prin- ciple of indirect taxation, the motion would strike a heavy blow at the proceedings of any Chancellor of the Exchequer, who should attempt to act upon that principle. (Ministe- rial cheers.) The Chancellor of the Exchequer had made a belti,` fide attempt to assert that taxation ought to be divided between direct and indirect taxation, and yet he was met by the most obstructive of all proceedings in the form of a motion again:t his bill. If an Administration were to be formed by hon. gentlemen opposite they would repent of this step, as well as of many others they had taken while the present Government were in office. (Cheers.) The member for North Devon would have nothing to do with ' the counter-Budget of the member for Gloucestershire. -end said the proposal of a tax upon tea was a mere illustration. What was the cause of this tremendous opposition to the Budget; It was in reality the death duties, in regard to which his right hon. friend had in- vaded the sanctuary of landed property. (Cheers) His right hon. friend had shown how mild his proposed arrangement now was ; but it was plain there were many points on which the quality would not be established. Ob- jection was taken with regard to the non-taxation of wine. It was said that the Government were favouring the foreigner. (Opposition cheers.) He asserted that there was no article in our tariff which had done so much to pro- mete,the interests, not of the foreigner, but of trade and in- dustry at home, as the article of wine. It had secured an opening for British industry to the extent of many millions ,Of trade per annum. It was a serious matter, therefore, to +touch tke subject, especially in view of the trifling amount that could be raised by that means. The tax upen wine. moreover, though moderate, was heavier than the tax sta beer. Although the present motion was made by the Con- servative Opposition, and although rash proposals were sup. posed to emanate from advanced parties, he did not think it had been,well considered, however unusual was the coarse the Opposition were now taking. There had been a mice'. site for great military preparations, which had in view to ward off a serious danger impending over the country. The Government now hoped that danger might pass away, but Irthey were not at this moment able to say it had passed away. It would be premature to say it, and they were still asking the House to grant them pecuniary means for bear- ing the cost of the preparations required. The prepara- tions had been sanctioned, and they asked the House to provide for the charge. The regular Opposi- tion, the loyal Opposition, the national Opposition—(laugh- ter) the patriotic Opposition (renewed laughter) the constitutional Opposition—(more laughter)—refused this money. This was a most unprecedented proceeding The right hon. gentleman supported the Vote of Credit for warlike preparations, and having done that be now refused the Government the means they asked for making the ,charge. The ancient usages of Parliamentary Oppoeitioo were to be abandoned by a party calling itself sometimes Conservative and sometimes Tory Democrat. (Laughter.) But the mover of this amendment was perfectly In- telligible. Liu used expressions again and again which had but one meaning. He said you ought to lay a tax on tea— stew on tea was so moderate. Let them consider what kind of moderation there was in it. A tax of 20 per cent. on beer was not considered very moderate, and an addition ,etC per cent. ,as looked upon as an intolerable imposition. The tax on tea,was not less than 48 per cent. at present, and murder to obtain the money required by the Government they must lay an additional tax of 3d. In the pound. The ' right hon. gentlaman said it was easy to readjust the Bud. get. If that was an, why did he not tell them how it was to be dope? It was idle to talk of this 'readjustment. What were they going to tarn? Were they going to tax raw materials of industry? Were they going to reimpose Protective duties? They might tax tea or reimpose the tax on sugar. (“Hear, beat," from Lord Randolph Churchill.) He rejoiced to come across a Irani. antagonist, with whom he could discuss in thelight of day, and who was not content to ekrink and cover himself behind assurances that it would be quite easy to readjust the Budget. That was the issue upon which the Goverment had made up their minds. It was a qaestion of life and death. As such the Government ac- cepted j and welcomed it, and they did not envy Hume who, if they gained the victory, would have to bear the conse- quences. (Ministerial cheers.) The House divided, when the numbers were— Fr the amendment 264 Against Majority against the Government 12 The annzuncement of the numbers was received with loud and prolonged cheer:lig by the Ooposition and the Irish members, many of whom stood on the benches, waving their hats, and shouting " Buckshot " and " Coer- cion." _ _ .

Mr. Gladstone con- cluded the'debate at half-past one o'clock on Tues- day morning, when a division was taken, with the result that Sir M. Hicks-Beach's amendment was carried by 264 against 252, a majority of 12 against the Government. The announcement of the figures was received with a joint demonstration on the part of the Tories and the Irishmen, and it was some time before the Speaker could put the amend- ment as a substantive motion. This having been put and carried, Mr. Gladstone moved the:adjourn- ment of the House forthwith, and this course was adopted, members rushing from the House in wild disorder and excitement.
