div.head: TIIE 'SCENE IN TIIE HOUSE.
div.p: TIIE 'SCENE IN TIIE HOUSE.

When the tellers came in from the Government lobby and there was still no appearance of the tel- lers from the Opposition lobby, excitement on the Opposition side grew. Lord R. Churchill and other Tory members isegan to clap their hands. They were almost beyond control in their excitement dur- ing the brief interval of waiting. As soon as the numbers from the Opposition lobby were brought in and made known privately, the Tories and the Irishmen rose en the benches cheered and waved 'their hats in frantic delight. It was several nun- sites before quiet was restored so that the numbers -could be announced to the House, when it was found that the Opposition had mustered 264, against .2.52 for the Government, giving a majority of 12 against the Government. Again, there was the wildest shouting and waving of hats on the Oppo- sition side, the Yemenites indulging in savage ex- ultant cries of "Buckshot," "Coercion," "Myles Joyce," mingled with calls for Gladstone. All the while the Premier was engaged in his usual occu- pation of writing. •Cir M. Hicks-Beach's amend- ment became the substantive motion, and was agreed to without another trial of strength. Then, when the Crofter's Bill, which stood ,next on the paper, was called on, there were crieslor "Glad-, stone," with More wild shouting when he rose to thelable. In a few words he moved the adjourn- ment of the House, and , the excited members at , once took themselves ..off, leaving the aight hon. ,gentloman still writing,on his knee. MEETING OP THE CABINET.

A Cabinet Council as-s-ani-bied at noon on Tuesday at the Premier's official residence. Only &Sew per- sons were present in Downing-street as the Minis- ters ,assonibled, and the ra.,jority of these were hn- mediately connected with Government offices. Earl Grauville.was the first to arrive, coming over to Downing-street from Carlteon House-terraee a few minutes before 12 o'clock, and Lord Rizosebety fol- lowed,immediately afterwards, Earl Spencenbeing the third to arrive, and, ultimately all the Ministers were present. While Ministers were assembling, Sir Peter,Lumsden passed tothe India Offioe.. Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote were in early communication with each other.

The Cabinet ,rose at a quarteryast one, Sir Charles Duke being the fast to leave, and proceeded direct to.the Local Government Board. Lords Derby and Rosebery followed almost immediately, and walked away together to Bt. James's-square. Sir William Harcourt drove home, and Lord Granville proceeded to the Foreign Offica. Lords Kimberley and Her- tington and Mr. Shaw Lefevre remained behind for 'some time, and did notleavetill nearly half an hour after the bulk of the Ministers. MI the members of the Government emerged from Mr. Gladstone's official residence, smiling and chatting pleasantly together as if nothing unpleasant had occurred. Immediately after the conclusion of the Council, special messages were despatched from Downing- street to the Reform Club and other Liberal centres, where it was subsequently positively asserted that Ministers had decided to place their resignation in the hands of her Majesty,. In certain quarters, however,, there was a disposition to believe a rumour to the effect that Ain Gladstone alone
would resign, and that the Ministry would be re- constructed. . , , , STATZMENT•__BY •THB_PREMIER.-_--ADJOIMN-
MENT OF BOTH HOUSES. HOUSE OF LORDS.-TIIRSDAY.
The Lord Chancellor took his; seat on the Wool- sack at 4-15. _ . _

_ There was some appearance of excitement in the body of the House,' and a small number of Peers occupied seats in the side galleries, but the visitors to the Strangers' Gallery did not number more than half a dozen, There were about 50 Peers seated on the opposite side, about 40 on the Ministerial side, and nine on the Cross Benches. Amongst those present were the Duke of Northumberland, the Duke of Marlborough, the Duke of Manchester, the Duke of Devonshire, the Duke of Buckingham, the Marquis of Salisbury, the Marquis of Tweedale, the Bishops of Oxford and Carlisle, the Duke of Argyle, the Marquis of Ripon, the .Earl of Kimberley, the Earl of Northbrook, the Earl of Rosebery, the Duke of Richmond, the Earl of Derby, the Earl of Redes- dale, Earl Spencer, the Earl of Camperdown, Lord Bramwell, the 'Marquis of Bristol, Earl Cowper, the Earl of Clarendon, the Earl of Belmore, Lord Napier of Magditla, the Earl of Wemyss, Earl Beauchamp, Lord Enfield, Lord Waveney, Lord Bury, Lord Inchiquin, Lord Houghton; Lord Sherbrooke, Lord Ravenworth, and Lord Winmarleigh.—Some peti- tions having been presented, private bills were ad- vanced a stage. THE DEFEAT OF THE GOVERNHENT.—EarI GRAN- VILLE rose, and said: My Lords,—Your lordships are aware, not only from the ordinary means of communication, but also by the decision of the House of Commons, communicated to this House, of what took place in that 'assembly last night. In consequence of that event, I have to move that your lordships do adjourn till Friday. Of course, the House will continue to sit for judicial buSineSs, and the Private Bill Committee will sit.—Lord BALFOUR of BIIIILEIGH I Will the Committee of Privileges meet to-morrow ?—Earl GRANVILLE : Yes.
The House adjourned at 4-35 until Friday. • HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuasnA. The Speaker took the chair a few minutes before 4-0.

The House rapidly filled, and before the usual time for commencing public business it was crowded in every part, the principal members on both sides being present. Shortly before half-past four o'clock' Mr. Gladstone entered the House, and was warmly cheered by his supporters. He was immediately followed by Sir M. Hicks-Beach, who was not less cordially received by the Opposition. PROVISIONAL ORDERS.—Mr. G. Russ Eta, moved the second reading of a bill to confirth certain Pro- visional Orders of the Local Hovernment Board re- lating to the Local Government districts of Inver- ston and the borough of Wigan.—The bill was read a second time, and referred to a 'Select Committee. The hon. gentleman also moved the second reading of a bill to confirm certain Provisional Orders of the Local Government Board under the provisions of the Divided Parishes aad Poor-law Amendment Acts 1876 and 1877 relating to the hamlet of War- rington.—The bill was read a 'second time, and re- ferred to a,Select Committee.
STATEMENT BY MIL GLADSTONE.-THE RE- DISTRIBUTION OF SEATS BILL.

At half-past four o'clock, Mr. GLADSTONE rose, and was again warmly cheered. He said: Sir,---tmmediately •on having arrived at the hour when public business usually commences, I rise for the' purpose of addressing a few words to the House, and I do so before any questions have, been addressed to mycolleagnes or to myself, on the ground that I perceive that some of those questions relate to the intentions and views of responsible Ministers: In consequence of the division of last night, the members of the Cabinet have consulted to-day, and have thought it their duty through me to submit a dutiful commu- • nication to her. Majesty. (Cheers and counter- cheers.) It would be altogether premature on my part to allude particularly to the nature of that communication—ka laugh from below the gangway on the Conservatrve side)—but I *ill say to the House—following the rule on former occasions, and. what, indeed, is obvious—that, some days must elapse before the result of the communication can be arrived at so as to be made a communication to the House. For these obvious reasons, and for the convenience and propriety following the established rule, that during an Interval of time of the nature of that before the House, the House should refrain from the transaction of ordinary 'business, I shill presume to act on that by maldng a motion to the effect that the House at its rising do adjourn to Fri- , day next. I snake this motion before making a mo- tion for the adjournment of the House, to allow an interval between the two motions; first, because it is no right of mine to prescribe the business of the House should attempt, but 'I humbly venture to recommend that the usual practice should be ad- hered to, inretead of going through the form of post- poning the orders of the day, 'because by the ordin- ary rules of the House those orders will reappear when the House reassembles, and then it will be within the Pleasure of the House to make a suita- ble arrangement respecting them. It would, how- ever, be desirable that the ustral motion should be made to allow the Committees to continue their sittings in the interval, therein also adhering to the established practice of Parliament. Under the cir- cumstances, sir, I have no more to say, and now make the motion—" That this House at its rising do adjourn to Friday next." Sir S. NORTHCOTE (who on rising was warmly cheered from the Conservative benches): I think that the course which the fight hon. gentleman pro- poses is, as he says, both convenient and usual. The only question I wish to ask him is this—l did not quite understand his intention—Will he, as soon as this motion should be adopted, then imme- diately move the adjournment of the House, or does he propose that other business shall be Carried on? I also wish to ask if he considers it likely there will be any business of special importance to be tran- sacted in connection with the Redistribution Bill which may be expected, I suppose, from the other House. I put this question because, as the House is aware, the Redistrilmtionliill ilea question in regard to which days are important. The Speaker then rosette put the motion. Mr. GLADaroNE : May I be allowed, sir, to reply to the Question put to me before you put the motion. I intended to make myself clear to this effect, that, although I have no right to go out of the usual course for the purpose 6f forcibly putting aside business, yet the recommendation I submitted to the House was that we shouldv.adjourn before the regu- lar business was entered upon. The reason for an interval after the first motion which is now in the hands of the Speaker simply is that it is usual and convenient to make a motion that committees may continue their sittings, notwithstanding the ad- journment of the House. She right hon. gentleman has referred to a point rff considerable importance, which had not escaped my notice, namely, whether we should reserve to ourselves discretion to ask the House to proceed with .any matter relating to the Redistribution of Seats 'Bill if the question arise. That, sir, did not escape our attention. I have to observe in the first place that' it does not depend upon us but upon the House of Lords to regulate its proceedings in such a way as to bring that subject before us or not. If the House ce Lords should think I fit to carry forward the Redistribution of Seats Bill, so as to cause it to reach this House on or before the time when the House re-assembles on Friday next, certainly then it wbuld be our duty to consider to advise the House to the best of our ability as to the propriety of proceeding to deal with any amendments which may be made in that bill bythe House of Lords. It would undoubtedly be an unusual proceeding only justified by a joint reference to two considerations. I One is that the other House of Parliament had thought fit to make a precedent on grounds which they conceived to be urgent public reasons for proceeding with particular -business, notwith- standing the adjournment of thellouse under peen- liar circumstances; and the other would be that we were of opinion that the circumstances were such that the need of going forward speedily with the Seats Bill was se urgent that, taken in conjunction with the general concurrence of opinion as to mat- ters embodied in the bill, made it our daty to raise the question, notwithstanding the peculiarity of the circumstances in which we stand. That question I had better reserve for the present, inasmuch as it cannot arise except in consequence of proceedings -avhich may or may not be taken in the other House, and in respect to which I have no authentic infor- mation. Indeed, that information is more likely to be in the possession of the right hon. gentleman , opposite than in mine. So far as any information has reached me, it is not to the effect that the House of Lords is likely to proceed with the bill in the inter- val between now and Friday. The /notion was then put and agreed to. Mr. fitLADsroun then moved that all Committees of the House have leave to sit, notwithstanding the adjournment of the House.—This was agreed to. Mr. GLADSTONE, rising again, said : Interpreting the silence of the House as consent, I now beg to move that this House do now adjourn. The motion was accepted, and. the House stood adjourned at 5-20.

div.head: FEELING IN LONDON.
div.p: FEELING IN LONDON.

„Tlae Press Association says :—The fact that the • Government had been defeated by 12 on the Budget appeared to come with the utmost surprise upon• all classes in the metropolis. , It was known that a determined effort would be made against any in- crease in the spirit duties, but the danger to the existence of the Government was not regarded as serious, in view of the various votes of censure during the present session. Consequently, when it wa.s learnt that the Ministry had succumbed to an adverse vote, and that there was a prospect of the immediate resignation of Mr. Gladstone and his col- leagues, much excitement was manifested among the tens of thousands of people pouring into the city on every side by tram, bus, and tranicar—it was the one topic of conversation. Opinions were greatly divided as to the probabilities of the imme- diate future. That Mr. Gladstone would tender the resignation of the Ministry to the Queen was uni- versally accepted as certain, in view of the intima- tioi . thrown out by Sir C. Mike and the Premier himself in the course of Monday night's debate. It was regarded as quite certain that her Majesty would then send for Lord Salisbury, with instruc- tions to form an administration; but at this point uncertainty began. Some Conservatives argued that it was impossible for their party to accept office under present circumstances, and that Mr. Gladstone would be called upon to resume the reins until the general election under the new franchise, which is practically certain to stake place in N.ov. A great number of Conservatives do not, however, coincide with these views, and express the opinion that, as their party has at length been victorious, they ought to reap the advantage by immediately assuming office. The bulk of the Liberals appear to agree in this, and they point to the fact that on& a month or two since, when a vote of censure was be moved, it was authoritatively announced that if successful the Conservative leaders would be ready to accept office. Among the Radicals, especially those belonging to the more advanced clubs, there is freely expressed the opinion that the defeat of the Gov- ernment will have one good effect, in that it will prevent a Liberal Cabinet from introducing any fur- ther coercive legislation with regard to Ireland, and these also state their hope that, even if the Conserv- atives decline to take office and Mr. Gladstone con- tinues Prime Minister, Sir Charles Dilke, Mr. Cham- berlain, and Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, who are known to have expressed in the Cabinet their objection to the renewal of the Crimes Act except under certain conditions, will refuse to rejoin the Administration except with a guarantee that the Crimes Act should be allowed to lapse and Ireland governed by the or- dinary law. Much activity is being displayed in the various Government offices to prepare for the eventuality of a new Administration coming into power; and at the great political clubs members eagerly discuss the possibilities of the situation. Matters are regarded as additionally complicated ia b the fact that no immediate dissolution can take ce as it could at ordinary times, owing to the distribution Bill not being passed and the new franchise not being in operation. 1 PROBABLE ResTURN OF THE QUEEN TO I

WINDSOR. The Daily News says Lord Hartington had made arrangements to go to Balmoral on Wednesday night in the stead of Mr. Gladstone, with the object of saving the Prime Mihister the fatigue of the long journey northwards, and for the purpose of affording her Majesty personally any ex- planation ehe might wish to receive as to the political situation. At a very late hour, however, the intention was abandoned, and Lord Hartington remains in London. The public inconvenience that accrues from the Queen's absence at Balmoral at the present crisis is so great that little doubt exists that her Majesty will return to London, in accord- ance with constitutional precedent. Mr. Gladstone and his colleagres are. pending acceptance of their resignation, re- aponsible for the conduct of public business. Most ef the Ministers were on Wednesday in attendance upon their official duties. Rumours were current on Wednesday of in- creasing hesitation on the part of the Conservative leaders with respect to taking office. It is quite true that more than one influential member of the party questious the ad- visability of the step. But we are in a position to re-affirm ocr statement of Tuesday that if office be offered to the Con- servative leaders they will accept it. It is understood at the Home Office that Sir Hicke-Beach is desirous of sue- ,ceeding Sir Wm. Harcourt. The statement that Sir BAliol Brett is to be the new Lord Chancellor has drawn from Sir Hardinge Giffard the expression of opinion that the office would more naturally fall to the former Solicitor-General of t,,e party returning to power. It is understood that Mr. Edward Clarke will be the new Attorney-General. Mr. Gorst will probably be Solicitor-General, unless he be made Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies. Prolonged de- lay in the appointment Of the new Ministry would, it is stated, be attended by highly inconvenient consequences in Egypt. One of the ,first duties of the new Ministry will be to ask for a further vote en account of Supply. On the 18th May a vote for three millions was taken. This sum was estimated to cower -six weeks, of which four will have elapsed on Monday next. Official notice is given that the State apartments of ,Windsor Castle will be closed until further orders.

The Press Association Says: It was rumoured in usually well-informed quarters that the Queen had wired to Mr. Gladstone asking him to reconsider his decision. There is, however, no reason to believe that the right hon. gentleman would consent, under present circumstances, to resume the responsibilities of office. One conclusive' reason against such a course, and one which has not previously been dis- closed, is that the Prime Minister is and has been in full accord with Sir Charles Dilke and Mr. Chamberlain in the indisposition to sanction even a partial renewal of the Crimes Act fer 'lreland except for a limited period and ac- companied by definite assurances of early remedial legisla- tion. It is therefore still expected that her Majesty will shortly send for the Marquis of Salisbury, who, it is gene- rally believed, will undertake to form an Administration to carry on the necessary business of the country until the general electicn. On Wednesday forenoon Mr. Gladstone was visited at his official residence by Earl Granville, the Marquis' of Hartington, Lord Rosebery, andother political associates and private friends. In the afternoon he went out for a drive with Mrs. Gladstone. The Marquis of Salis- bury and Sir Stafford Nordnote also received visits in the course of the day from a number of their leadhag Parlia- mentary followers, but no formal conference of the Conser- vative leaders was held, nor will any meeting of the party I be summenedst present. A large informal meeting of Con- servative members of both Houses was held on Wednesday between four and five o'clock at the Carlton Club. Neither Lord Salisbury nor Sir Stafford Northcote were present, but many prominent members, including Lord Randolph Churchill, whose names have been mentioned in connection with seatsin the Cabinet attended the meeting. The Evening Standard for Wednesday says :—We are in a position to state authoritatively tbat,in the event of heing entrusted ky the, Queen with the task of forming a Minis- try, the Conservative leaders will be ready to undertake the duty. United ',viand on Thursday published an" interview " with its proprietor, Mr. Parnell, on the political crisis. The bon. member for Cork is reported te have said that he could have driven the Government from power long ago but for the abstention of nominal members of his party. He believes that by the victory on Tuesday morning he has saved the only remaining Dish industry from a heavy tam and put an emit, coercion for ever. The frisk Times says that there are many among the Parneilite party who regard Tuesday morning's division as a Pyrrhic victory, and who consider, to quote the words of one of them. that they have wrecked the Ministry before their own lifeboats were ready. In those Ulster constitu- encies in which, though the Nationalists felt themselves linable to run candidates of their own, they believed them- selves able to turn the tide, it bad been arranged that the Nationalist electors should be advised to vote for the Con- servative candidates. But now the Nationalists of the North are required to hold themselves absolutely neutral.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
REPORTED ASSASSINATION OF THE AMEER OF

AFGHANISTAN. S. Prrnatitte&O, SiTURDAY.—The Novosti has received private information from the Caucasus that Abdurrahman, the Ameer of Afghanistan, has been assassinated by his priests. Abdurrahman was recognised as Ameer at Cabal by the British, and proclaimed on July 22nd, 1880. Ayoob Khan, who seems to have become the object of the solicitude of the Russian Government, was interned in Per- sia, where he now remains, closely guarded. SIMLA, SUNDAY.—The Indian Gavernment has no know- ledge whatever of the alleged assassination of the Ameer of Afghanistan reported yesterday by the St. Petersburg Novosti TIFLIS, SITNDA.Y.—No news has been received here con- firming the reported assassination of the Ameer of Afghanis- tan.

ST. PETEROCIRG, TIIVESDAY.—The Nouosti to-day states that the rumour of the assassination of the Ameer of Afghanistan is persistently current, not only in the Caucasus but on the Afghan frontier. The journal also announces the receipt of intelligence from the Caucasus reporting from sources described as well informed that excitement exists in Afghanistan.___

div.head: ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.
div.p: ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.

ST. PETERSBURG, SUNDLY.—It is understood that an agreement in principle has been arrived at with regard to the question of the Zulficar Pass. It has been decided to leave the command of what is known as the Zulficar Pass in the bands of the Afghans, but the exact point te which the Ameer's territory will extend is to be fixed by the Joint Commission in such way as will ensure to the Russians a reasonable, or, in other words, a defen- sible position at the end of the pass. There is no con- firmation of the rumour that the Ameer has been assassi- nated. TEHERAN, SUNDAY.—lntelligence received here states that the Governor of Herat has sent some men to Bala Murghab, and is now patching up the fortification of the city. Intelligence from Mery states that strangers are not allowed to mix with the Turcomans, and are required te ream, in quarters provided for them by the Russian authorities. Some Persians, believed to be in correspond- ence with Afghans and others, have been removed from Merv. _ _

CRONSTADT, Sugnar.—A equadron, composed chiefly of gunboats and torpedo vessels, commanded by Admiral Kopitoff, sailed yesterday on a cruise off the Esthonian coast. It will also explore the channels near the islands of Dagoe, Oessel, Worms, and Moen. The Press Association is in a position to state that the Anglo-Russian negotiations on the Afghan frontier question will remain in their present almost complete state pending the decision of the Queen as to a change of Go- vernment.

Colonel Stewart, assistant Afghan Commissioner, who reached London on Tuesday evening, brings important despatches for Sir Peter Lumsden, by whom he had been deputed with Major Holditch and Colonel Peacock to in- spect the fortifications of Herat. At that city Col. Stewart and party were received with marked honour by the Afghan authorities.

div.p: EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN.

From General Lord Wolseley : " Canto, 6rm JUNE, 1895.—Buller reports from Dongola that detachment Naval Brigade left Fatmeh yesterday in three whalers. 7,225 refugees have left. Col. Butler and all mounted troops have reached Dongola and all stations soath of Dongola are now evacuated:" _ _

ALEXANDRIA, SATURDAIL—The Iris sailed to-day under sealed orders. The Duke and Duchess of Connaught bay- ing performed quarantine at Suez, have proceeded through the Canal on their way to Marseilles. The Khedive and his family arrive here for the summer on Monday next. The Mandi is now at Korti, and is preparing to advance on Dongola as soon as the British troops are with- drawn.

817ME1151, SONDAY.—Last evening a party of rebels ap- peared a considerable distance from here, and fired shots at the water forts. They then retired. A spy, whose informa- tion is believed to be trustworthy, has come in here, and confirms the report of the scarcity of food and the spread of smallpox amongst the tribes as far as Kassala and Berber. This combination of evils is causing rapid desertion among the followers of Osman Digma and the latandi. The rebels whe are besieging Kassala are said to be retiring for the same reason.

_ Salonica announces that a detachment of Tartish troops and gendarmerie have encountered in the mountains'? ' Kodja Balkan, in the province of Kossova, a band of 80 Bulgarian brigands from the district of Kustemlje. A sanguinary cortlict ensued, in which the brigands suffered severely, their chief, Tasbro, being captured. THE EARTHQUAKE IN CASHMERE. &ma, SAvunnev.—The British Resident in Cashmere reports to-day that shocks of earthquake continue to be felt in that revince. I several places the earth opened and swallowed up houses, while hot water and clouds of ,stel. phurous dust were ejected from the chasms. These phe- nomena were accompanied by loud subterranean rumbling. Generally speaking, the movement of the earth has been comparatively slight. THE RISING IN CANADA. TORONTO, SUNDAY—General Middleton telegraphs that four prisoners, who have escaped from Big Bear's hands to General Strange's camp, report that no indignities are being offered to any of the women by the Indians. Big Bear's band is broken up into two parties, and these are escaping by different trails, both of which are being followed by the Canadian troops. OTTAWA, MONDAL—Fifty-one prisoners who were car- ried off by Big Bear have escaped and have reached General Middleten's camp. Only one of Mr. M*Lean's family now remains a prisoner. Big Bear is retreating. OTTAWA, WEDNESDAY.—AII Big Bear's prisoners from Fort Pitt have been released ; Mrs. Delaney and Mrs. Gowanlock are among the number, and have not been mal- treated.

div.head: REPORTED FALL OF KA.SSALA.
div.p: REPORTED FALL OF KA.SSALA.

CAIRO, MONDAY.—A telegram has been received here to- day, from Soakim, stating that a man has come in who says that Kassala has fallen. There is reason to believe that no massacre has occurred. The information secured is scanty, but the news is believed to be true. This brave garrison was no doctlit forced to surrender for want of provisions The fall of Kassala will unquestionably enable Osman Dig= to obtain reinforcement, with which he will rene his attack on Suatirs. Another man arrived in Snakim yesterday, having taken 25 days to travel there from Berber. lie says there is one European in Berber. This is believed to be Cozzi. the friend of General Gordon. The man far- ther states that wheat is only sold in Berber at famine prices.

div.p: FRANCE AND CHINA.

Pants, TCESDAY.—M. de Freycinet, Munster f6r Foreign Affairs, announced to-ay in the Cuamber of Deputies that a despatch had been received from M. Patenotre, French Minister to China, stating that the treaty between France and China bad been signed at four o'clock this afternoon at Tientsin.
DESTRUCTIVE WATERSPOUT IN MEXICO.-100

PERSONS DROWNED. New York despatches from Jalisco, Mexico, report that the district around that town was last Sunday devastated by a tremendous waterspout, which, bursting over the mountains, swept down the valley in an irresistible torrent. Houses and other structures were swept away; the valley was completely flooded ; and it is estimated that at least 109 persons were drowned.

THE SUEZ CANAL COMMISSION. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—The British Ministerial crisis has strengthened the belief already positively en!ertained that the Suez Canal Commission will break up without deci,iing for or against the rival versions of clause 10, concerning the question of international control. The draft treaty contain- ing the different proposed versions of this clause will ba submitted to the Powers, who will deal diplomaticaly with the questions at issue. COLLISION ON THE SUEZ CANAL.

IsmattAA, WEDNESDAY. 8-5 P.M.—A Suez Canal Com- pany's dredger and the Thomas Melville have been In collision. The former vessel sank; the latter is slightly damaged. The collision has stopped the traffic in the Ctnal temporarily. TERRIBLE DISASTER IN FRANCE.-20 PERSONS _ KILLED AND 60 INJURED. _

PARIS, TIRTBSDAY.—A fatal accident is reported from Tillers, in the Department of Puy de Dome, where the Etair- case of the Court-house gave way, killing 20 persons aud injuring about 60 others. An Exchange Company's telegram, dated Paris, Thurs- day, states :—An awful catastrophe is reported this morn- ing in telegrams from Thiers, in the Department of Puy de Dome. A trial for murder took place there yesterday, and the court was crowded. At the close of the proceedings. those persons who had been present were leaving the build- ing, when ths staircase, which was built of stone, fell, kill- ing or maiming those who were beneath it, and also those who fell with the heavy masses of stonework. When the panic was over, the work of removing the dead and wounded commenced. The latest telegrams say that 20 dead bodies had been taken from the ruins, and between 80 and 90 in- jured. Many of the wounded are so terribly injured that their recovery is hopeless.

as held Ononui nTn announced, arfioaurybtl hiwcee Hall, moll-seeae—rotdifns-gh:aonwTs-i-std.therare.ieng Liberalatsh ea already mb' inewita.; ; tion of the council that Colonel David Gamble be adopted as the Liberal candidate for the borough. Mr. R. Pilkiegton , presided. The meeting was held in private, reporters being excluded. We understand that a large number of questions . were put, and in reply, ; Colovel Gamble said be could not see any objection to the passing of a county government bill, whereby a council duly ' elected by the ratepayers on the one-man one-vote principle I should be empowered to appoint borough and county magis- trates, but he thought the liquor trade should be I regulated locally, and net by a county council. With regard to the Irish question, he thought it was a misfortune that there were separate laws for each of the countries comprising the United ; Kingdom, and he was of the same opinion as Mr. Parnell that there should be equal laws for the three coun- tries. On tins subject of inc ,me-tax beheld the same opinion as his father, namely, that all men receiving wages to the extent of 20s a week and upwards should be compelled to pay income-tax and thereby be entitled to a vote. He would certainly vote for an inquiry into the private en- closures acts, which had been passed during the past fifty ' ?mars, as he believed they had been the cause of great in- justice. Adverting to the disestablishment question, he said as the Church in %Vales did not altogether represent the religion of the people, he would stretch a point and vote for disestablishment. But in regard to the English Church he was bound to tell them that he was not in favour of the severence of the Church from the State unless some pro- vision for the worship of God was made by the State in another form. He pleaded ignorance of the provisions of the amendment to the mines regulaction act, but after they were explained to him he remarked I that the weighing clauses especially were reasonable. . Asked if It WAS a fact that he had been to London to oppose the bill for the promotion of a railway from Sr. Helrna to ; Wigan, Colonel Gamble replied that he had nothing what- ; ever to do with the project pro or con., although he should be glad to see the new railway laid. He would , not vote for the abolition of the House of Lords At j the same time he thought the number of members conetie tuting the upper Chamber should be reduced considerably, ' say to one-third. and should be elected from the prerage by the people. He expressed himself in favour of a measure for the abolition of primogeniture settlement and entail, and gave his acquiescence in the introduction of an im-• I proved and revised law with reference to the responsibilttv lof employers in case of injury to workmen. He had no• fixed opinion on the subject of the payment of the members of Parliament, but he was rather in favour of it. At the conclusion of his speech Colonel Gamble retired from the room, and in his absence a long discu-sion took j place. On the motion of Dr. M`Nicoll, seconded by Mr. J.. Birchall, Colonel Gamble WAS adopted as the Liberal cold'- , date for the borough.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1885.

nIT is the unexpected which happens; the Li°vernment were defeated early on Tuesday `4oroing on a paltry budget proposal, and the et°llntry is now in the throes of a political tlisis• What a curious commentary it is on , *ke, fortunes of political warfare that a Cabinet ; 441 ch has successfully resisted an untold ; htllalber of Votes of Censure on its general rhlicY should be brought down on the narrow gre whether a tax, admitted to be necessary, tr,°llld be laid on Beer or Tea! It brings ttlind ByRON'S famous description of the tath of the "military commandant 7,— And such an end! that he who many a day had faced Napolean's foes until they fled— The foremost in the charge or in the sally, 1.11 Should now be butchered in a civic alley! th e Government have been defeated, but eY have not been discredited, and this is Pinte than can be said of their opponents, or senile of their nominal supporters. It is 116'4 deep regret—it is with a feeling of tta'nie that we perceive that the greatest tit s 'estnan of the age, and the best Ministry ov4t this country has e'er seen, have been erthrown through the indifference or negli- gbert„ ott4i'e of so-called friends, rather than by th,t it p:lsight of acknowledged foes. How comes th n•Lat so many Liberals were absent from alwe'r Places on Monday night? Illness hqtaTs accounts for a number being away, tinere were as many absent when they tori4ld have been present—not taking into ac- the-ttt the "pairs "—as would have converted ititoloajority of twelve against the Government ku a majority of three or four times that Of To • We need hardly say that, the name 014 RX GORDON MCMINNIES is not amongst half-hearted who are to be found any- Akre but in the ranks in the hour of con- the i It is well that the list is published of theugn,?ble deserters of a truly noble leader; tb,t3' will have to r,ckon with their constitu- the and we trust that when the crush comes Will be found amongst the weak who tor have to go to the wall. We have not kalotten that all the trouble the Government th on the BRADLADGII question arose 9h divisig the abstention, at the first critical Kinn' Of the same, or a similar body of "141 Poltroons. If these men had had

peculiar convictions on the question of taxa- tion, and had shown the courage of their convictions in voting against the Govern- ment, we should have had some respect for them; but we have none for the nondescripts who are "neither fish, nor flesh, nor rood red herring." They are " wastrels," and should be weeded out at the next election. On the principle—if there is any prin- ciple in it—that all is fair in love, war, and electioneering, the Opposition may, from their own point of view, be justified in combining as they did with the PARNELLITES to overturn the Government on the Budget proposals. And yet it is a sorry business i it will not bear looking into. In the first place there was an admitted necessity for raising the money. If the Tories have shown them- selves more anxious about one thing than another it is that the Government should spend large sums on military armaments and military preparations. They were unanimous in agreeing to the Vote of Credit; but they back out, or endeavour to back out, when they are called upon to make good their words by levying the requisite taxes. It may, however, be said that they do not object to taxation, but to the particular tax on spirits and beer, whilst wine remains untouched. That is the form the resolution took—a reso- lution on which they were agreed when it came to voting, though there was no agree- ment in the arguments by which they sought to support it. Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH, the nover, conscious that it was part of his case to show how the money to be obtained from the tax on spirits and beer could be got in another way, boldly referred to tea as a more suitable article for further taxation, and even went the length of insinuating that the Govern- ment had not taxed tea because of their regard for the Radical teetotaller. Sir CHARLES DILKE promptly and aptly replied that, if such considerations had to be intro- duced in the debate, he did not hesitate to say that he preferred the Radical teetotaller to the pot-house politician. But he did more than rebuke the Tory leader; he made him look ridiculous by showing how monstrous it was to suggest an additional tax upon tea, already taxed so per cent. on the wholesale value, while the tax upon beer about which he was so anxious was only zo per cent. Later on, Mr. GLADSTONE pulverised the proposal of Sir M. BEACH when he said that, to obtain from tea the money required. "you must lay on a tax of not less than threepence a pound in addition to the present sixpence—that is to say, you must raise the tax to 75 per cent., and that on a beverage of universal consump- tion by the people, because you will not allow us to lay an additional 3 per cent. to the 20 per cent. on beer." Sir STAFFORD NORTH- COTE, in closing the debate on behalf of the Tory party, urged that the reference to taxing tea was simply an illustration; but, as he was not able to name any other article by way of illustration as a fit subject of taxation, it goes before the country, as it went before the House of Commons, that, if the Tories come into office, as they will if they are not in a state of utter collapse, their scheme of finance is to add 25 per cent. to the price of Tea in order to prevent 3 per cent. being added to the price of Beer! It used to be said that the Tories were the champions of the Beer-barrel and the Bible; they still stand by the Barrel, but they seem to have dropped the Bible, and with it not a little regaid for morality and common sense. Tea being at the present day an article of use in every household, we submit that to put a heavy tax 'on it in order to prevent a light tax on beer would be a piece of legislative iniquity of the very worst kind. It is a sound principle of political economy to tax the luxuries rather than the necessaries of life. There was a time when tea was regarded in this country as a luxury, and as such it was heavily taxed. It is now looked upon as one of the neces- saries of life, and, thanks to Mr. GLADSTONE and the Liberal party, the tax upon it has been .gradually reduced. Beer and spirits are luxuries, and—unlike tea—they are luxuries which, unhappily, result in more mischief to the human race than plague, pestilence; and famine. They are taxed, and not improperly taxed; but there is a hue and cry because the Government, in a case of extreme pressure, would add 3 per cent, to the tax on beer. The Tories, through Sir MICHAEL HICKS- BEACH, profess to be wiser and more equita- ble; they have rushed to the rescue of the brewer; they would spare him the 3 per cent., and to do this they would put 23 per cent. on tea. "Wonderful, and yet again, wonderful !"

THE Annual Report of the Medical Officer of Health for the Borough of Warrington, which was submitted to the Town Council at its last meeting, is on the whole a very satis- factory document. Notwithstanding the epidemic of measles which visited this part of the county, and which in Warrington carried off ioB children under five years of age, the death rate for the year is, contrary to general expectation, a little lower than that of the year previous, being z i•l9 per 1,000 for 184 as against 21.61 for 1883. The mortality from measles alone was just over two in the i,OOO, so that if the town had been spared the epidemic the death rate would have been exceptionally low. It may be replied that it is the usual order of things for there to be excessive mortality from one cause or another; but there is some little consolation in the reflection as to the mortality from measles that it .did not arise from anything peculiar to Warrington. St. Helens, Earles- town, Widnes, and Runcorn have also suffered from the same scourge. These are facts which should .be borne in mind in consider- 'jug this question of infant mortality. From some remarks that were made in the Council Chamber, it might be erroneously inferred that Warrington occupied a "bad eminence" amongst Lancashire towns for the large num- ber of deaths amongst children. But such is not the fact. We have pointed to a particular and exceptional cause as affecting the death rate for last year, and, more especially, the last quarter of the year. When we turn to the first quarter of the present year, we find a different because a normal state of things. From the Quarterly Return of the Registrar- General for the quarter ending March 3ist, 885, we learn that "the rate of infant mor- tality, measured by the proportion of deaths under one year to registered births, was 144 'per r,000." This is the average for the whole of England for the first quarter of the present year. But Warrington for the same period is considerably below this average, the number being 13z, as against 144. Even Southport is higher—i&; Wigan stands at 150, while St. Helens (with a high death rate from measles in January) reaches 184. There is no need therefore to single War- rington out as a town exceptionally destruc- tive to infant life ; it is bad in this respect— just as other manufacturing towns are bad; but so far as this year has gone it proves to be better rather than worse than its neigh-

div.head: EXA.MINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1885.
div.p: THE EXA.MINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 13, 1885.

Mr. Kirkham Evans, late of Runcorn. ha been elected one of the honorary secretaries of the Adelaide (Australia) Young Men's Christian Association. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—As open air meeting in connection with this society was held on the promenade on Thursday evening. A number of members walked in procession from the school to the place of ineetinge headed by the banner and brass band. Addresses were delivered upon temperance topics. ACCIDENT To A COMMISSIONERS' SERVANT.—Rich ard Austin, a man employed by the Board of Commissicners to cleau lamps, placed a vessel containing paint near to a gas light on Monday, when the oils in the paint ignited, and the flames scorched his face in a paint ul fashion and slightly injured his eyes. BRUNSWICK SUNDAY ScilooL, RUNCORN.—The anniver- sary services of this, the oldest selaool in .the town, are an- nounced to take place on Sunday, the 28th June. The Rev. IJames Hind, formerly of the Rancorn circuit, will occupy the pulpit on Sunday, and on Monday evening the Rev. C. Garret, of Liverpool, will preach. MODEL OF RUNCORN.—An historical relic in the shape of a model of a portion of the docks at Runcorn, made pro- bably at the time of their construction in the latter part of the last century, has been discovered at Worsley Hall. The model is in the possession of the Bridgewater Trustees. We understand that an application will be made by the Runcorn Free Public Library Committee to the Trustees for them to allow it to be placed among other curiosities as the nucleus of a museum. Mums HILL, Itunconee—The memorial to the Mmquis of Cholmondeley respecting this historic landmark has not yet elicited any reply to the Commissioners' request. In the meantime quarrying operations are proceeding vigor- ously. From the summit of the rock there is a precipice at least 80 feet deep, to ;he bottom of the quarry, and the spot is highly dangerous. The precaution has, however, been taken to place up a railing. A CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE FOR WIDNES —II is stated that the county Conservatives have requested Mr. Robert Pierpoint, barrister-at-law, who has taken a somewhat prominent part in Warrington politics, to contest Widnes in the Conservative interest. Whether Mr. Pierpoint has accepted the invitation or not we are unable at present to ascertain, but it is generally regarded that he would be leading a forlorn hope in contesting Widnes. LIBERALISM AT RUNCORN.—Every preparation is being made by the local Liberal Council for the struggle that is to take place at the next general election, and confident hopes are expressed that the long spell of Tory domination in the constituency will be broken The town has been divided into seven wards, each presided over by an able and energetic chairman, and this division of labour will greatly facilitate the electoral machinery with good results. Ar- rangements have been made for Mr. Brunner, the Liberal candidate, to address the electors of each ward on early dates. GOOD TEMPLARY AT Wrimees.—The ordinaay weekly meeting of the members of the Samaritan Lodge, 1.0 G.T., was held on Monday evening. Mr. Morris Jones, District Electoral Deputy, of Liverpool, occupied the chair, and in an address urged upon those present the necessity Of unity in all matters aff-cting the cause of temperance. He also advocated the appointment of a "Constituent Deputy" for Widnes, the duty of the deputy being to superintend the lodges in the town, on political and other questions. Bro. Pearson, P.W.C.T., was elected to the position. The usual routine business was transacted. Pro-Nrc FROM WIDNES.—The choir of St. Mary's Catholic Church had their annual picmic on Wednesday. About 30 members, accompanied by the Rev. Fathers Clarke, Old- ham, and Brennan, departed for Chester in the morning, and eh arriving at the ancient city, the cathedral and other objects of historical interest were viewed and inspected. The party then proceeded by boat to Eaton Hall. In the grounds of the mansion, rich with foliage and bright flowers, a pleasant afternoon was spent, the weather being beautifully flee. The return journey was made in the evening, the excursion having been thoroughly enjoyed. A RUNAWAY Homy AT WIDNES --Widnee-road was the scene of an exciting episode on Wednesday evening. A large open van belonging to Mr. Daniel Widgang, furniture dealer, Park-road, Liverpool, was left standing in front of Mr. Hurst's shop, Widnes-road, whilst the men in charge traneacted some business inside. Through some unknown cause the horse attached to the shafts started off at a furi- ous pace, and it was seen that a child about three years of age was in a somewhat perilous position in the vehicle. A crowd of men and women ran after the startled horse in a highly excited condition, and hoarse shouts and screams were heard. Opposite Dr. Cooper's residence in Albert-road a youth named Thomas Wycherley, who lives at 28, Wil- liam-street, and is employed at Widnes foundry, jumped at the horse's head, seized the bridle, and brought the animal to a standstill at the imminent risk of his own safety. He was warmly applauded by the assembled people, and the child was placed in the father's arms quite uninjured. CORPUS CHRISTI FESTIVAL AT DITTON.—The Church of St. Michael's, Ditton, was crowded with a large congre- gation on Sunday on the occasion of the festival of Corpus Christi. The edifice was decorated with flowers, and bright- ened by a display of banners and flags bearing various ecclesiaetical emblems. Owing to the unpropitious state of the weather the procession confined its perambulations to , the church, so that the altars and triumphal arches which had been erected in the college grounds were useless. The Sacred Host was borne in the procession by the rector, the Rev. Charles Wiedenmann, whose assistants were the Revs. Fathers Knabenbauer and Granderath. The children of St. Mary's Schools and a large number of the members of the Widnes League of the Cross took part in the proceed- ings. Seventy members of the Warrington Total Absti- nence League held a position in the procession. The stu- dents of the college, with the priests attired in copes and chasubles, preceded the host. The sermon was preached by the Rev. Father Rigby, of St. Francis Xavier's College' Liverpool. The ceremony of the benediction was performed at the high altar at the close. A CLEVER IMPOSTER AT Rtnecoate—A young man named John William Rigby, alias Thomas Mottersheed, alias Whittaker, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court on Thursday charged with obtaining money by false pre- tences. Superintendent Leah made a statement to the effect that the prisoner travelled about the country obtaining money from charitably disposed gentlemen by means of false statements. He had called at the houses of gentlemen in the neighbourhood. and expressed the deepest gratitude to the inmates for kind assistance be alleged had been ren- dered to him in the past, concluding by making a farther' demand upon their bounty. He repretented that be bad lost an arm whilst following his employment upon the railway at Warrington, and that he was desirous of raising a suffi- cient sum of money to purchase an artificial limb. In this manner be had obtained 10s from Mr Henry Stanton, J.P., of Thelwall ; 55 from Mr. James Marston, J.P., of Hill Cliffs; and 5s from Mrs. Hazleturst, of Beaconsfield House, Higher Runcorn. At Mr. Stanton's the prisoner also re- ceived a quantity of clothing, which he sold and pawned at Widnes, squandering the money thus obtained in getting drunk. The police have also ascertained that the prisoner had pawned at Northwich a silver lever watch bearing the number 6102, and the maker's name, Joseph Ball, London- road, Liverpool.—The pi isoner admitted having received the sums of money mentioned, and asked that he might be dealt with at once, leaving the watch out of consideration.— The magistrates, however, remanded the prisoner, who com- menced his career in an industrial school, and has been seven times convicted, until Monday, so that further iriquiries may be made. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fort- nightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dntten Workhouse, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Lieuten. ant-Colonel Ashton, there being also present Mr. John Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, and Messrs John Mclntyre, Themes Hadfield, James parr. William Pickering, John Efighfield, J. G Hamilton, J. G. Bryant, C. Mounfield, Dr. Adams (medical officer), H Linae Jeer (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy-clerk.)—A letter was read from the Loral Government Board sanctioning until the 25th March, 1886, the re.appointment of Mr. Jos. Adams as medical officer of health for the Authority's dis- trict, at a salary of £l2O pee annum—The Medical Officer reported on the spread of infectious diseases in the Author- ity's district. In Halton there were upwards of 20 cases of measles, and as the disease was rapidly spreading, mainly by school infection, he had recom- mended the closing of the schools, the attendance having fallen to 30 per cent. of the average. In Daresbury there was one case of scarlet fever, in Uelsby four, and at Frod- sham Bridge there was one. In Frodeham cases of measles were numerous, and the disease coutinned to spread Letters were received from various school managers in Frodsham agreeing to a request to close the Sunday schools for a Period while the measles epidemic is so severe.—Mr Far- rington, inspector, reported on several maters, and stated that a brook at Helsby had become polluted. He was directed to prepare a full report on the matter. A case of over-crow ling was reported at Norley. and notice was ordered to be served for the offence to be discontinued.— This was all the business. THE Liberals of St. Helens have made a good and timely choice in selecting Colonel GAMBLE as their candidate for the representa- tion of the borough at the forthcoming General Election. He is not a stranger to the town; he has served the Corporation in almost every responsible capacity, and is eminently fitted as a successful business man to make a useful member of Parliament. He has not yet appeared before the general body of the electors, but from the report which reaches us of the proceedings of the" Liberal zoo "of St. Helens, there can be no question as to:his receiving the enthusiastic support of the party. Colonel GAMBLE is not, like the Tory candidate, afraid of reform; nor does he shirk the issues that are placed before him. He sees the necessity of a county government measure which will place power where it ought to rest—in the hands of the people; and he would adopt the same prin- ciple in dealing with the licensing question. Irishmen will find in him a representative who will be anxious to redress their wrongs, for he would vote in favour of making equal laws for the three countries. He thinks the English Church should be disestablished, at any rate, in Wales, and it goes without saying that he is favourable to reform of the House of Lords. He would vote, too, for the abo- lition of the law of primogeniture, and the amendment of the Employers' Liability Act. Let the working-men of St. Helens contrast the programme of Colonel GAMBLE with that of Mr. SETON-KARR ; it is the difference between cheese and chalk.

LAST night Mr. GLADSTONE, in the House of Commons, and Lord GRANVILLE, in the House of Lords, formally announced that the QUEEN had accepted the resignation of the Government, and that Lord SALIS- BURY has been summoned to Balmoral. There is some uncertainty as yet as to whether Lord SALISBURY will ' accept office, though it is generally thought that he will attempt to carry on the Government of the coun- try until the dissolution of Parliament. Already it is beginning to be acknowledged in Conservative circles that it is an easier matter to say what should be done as to Ireland than to do it. It is stated that Lord SALISBURY and Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL were dining together when Her Majesty's summons to Balmoral reached Lord SALISBURY. Can it be that they were trying to find a way out of the difficulty in which they find themselves the one pledged to coercive measures, and the other committed to opposing the renewal of the Crimes Act ? It is not in the way of either of them to stick at " eating one's own words ;" the problem is to determine whose words shall be eaten. There is reason to believe that, if the Tories come into office, they will have no hesitation about renewing the Crimes Act, providing they can obtain the support of what are called moderate Liberals. It is to be hoped that no section of the Liberal party will walk into a Tory ;trap, however nicely it may be baited. The SALISBURY- CHURCHILL party have longed pined for an opportunity of showing what) they can do. Now that their chance has come, let them have plenty of rope; they will soon hang themselves.

-- WIDNES C.E.T.R.—The minstrel troupe of this organisa- tion, and several friends numbering, in all about 50 per- sons, had a trip to Southport on Saturday. The arrange- ments were admirably carried out by Mr. T. Davies, and the weather being beautifully fine, an enjoyable time was spent at the charming watering place. Horrouns FOR Loner. Musiciates.—Among the candi- dates who succeeded in satisfying the Examiner to the Royal Academy of Music on the occasion of his recent visit to Liverpool, in pianoforte music, were Miss Bertha Hankinson and Miss Edith Crosby, of Runcorn, the former of whom passed with honours, and the latter in the junior division. WIDNES ATHLETES AT ROUTHPORT.—At the athletic sports at Southport on Saturday the balf-mile flat race was won by T. Laws, of the Widnes Harriers, who received 47 yards start. In the 220 yards hurdle race handicap, S. Morris, of Widnes, with six yards, took the second place ; while in the quarter mile flat race handicap, D. A. Harding, Widnes, with 24 yards, was third. TRAP ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—As Mr. John Scannell, the relieving officer, was driving up Victoria-road on Mon- day afternoon in a trap belonging to Mr. Connor, the con- -1 veyance upset near the police station. Mr. Scannell was 'thrown violently to the ground, his face and other parts of his body being seriously injured. He was conveyed in a cart to the surgery of Dr. MacLennan, who attended to his wounds. MILTON LITERARY AND FRATERNAL ROCIETY.—Under the auspices of this society, and in aid of the funds of the Milton Congregational Chapel, Widnes a miscellaneous concert was given in that edifice on Tuesday evening. An audience of very modest proportions assembled, and Mr. E. Carey took the chair.—ln a brief address the Chairman re- marked that during the session 28 meetings had been held, and lectures, essays, and impromptu speeches had been delivered on a variety of topics. He referred with gratifica- tion to the fact that the society was nnsectarian, and con- cluded by pointing out the advantages to be derived from such a society. A long programme of vocal and instrumen- tal music had been provided, and the following ladies and 1 gentlemen took part :----Misses Palmer, Travis, Hudson, and A. Travis Messrs. J. Lea, F. Lea, T. ,Bowden, T. Wilson, 'Hoyle, Brown John Lea, Stirk, Jones (Runcorn), W. John- son, and J. Williams. Nor- man, Coleburn, Whittaker, Rogerson, Littler, and Salkeld (secretary.) The interments for the two months ended the 25th May were 75,corresponding period last year 61, increase 14. The fees received durine the same period amounted to £694s 6d ; last year £66 12s lid; increase £2 lie 7d.— The report of the Finance Committee?' adopted on the motion of Mr. Moss, showed that the receipts for the month amounted to £36 14 3d, and after paying wages £27 6s 3d had been paid into bank. Accounts amounting to £lB 15s 8d were passed for payment, and it was reported that interest amounting to £3l 17s 5d had fallen due.—A notice was ordered to be served upon the overseers to call a rate- payers' meeting on the 25th ult. to elect three members to the Board in place of Messrs. P. Briscoe, W. Whittaker, and W. Mellor, who retired, but were eligible for re-appoint- ment. SENTENCE ON A WIDNES MAN.—At the Liverpool See- alone, on Tuesday, David Evans, 63 years of age, labourer, was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment for having, at Widnes, on the 28th April, unlawfully and maliciously wounded Thomas Cosgrove. RUNCORN OLD HALL —The site of this ancient residence which is supposed to have been built in the 16th century, having been purchased by the Salvation Army for the erec- tion of a barracks, the building will shortly be removed. Mr. Pickets, of Bridge-street, has arranged to photograph the interesting relic before its destruction. THE COMMISSIONERS' LAW CLERK'S BILLS.—The bill of costs by Mr. W. H. Linaker' law clerk, against the Board of Commissioners, to which Mr. R. Shaw took exception at the monthly meeting, was passed by the Board in Corn- mittee. A committee was, however, appointed with the ob- ject of arriving at a more satisfactory arrangement with the law clerk.

A WARNING TO VAGRANTS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court on Monday William Dwyer was charged with sleeping in Messrs. Muspratt and Sons' chemical works. On Sunday morning the prisoner was found near the fur- nace boiler by P.C. McDonald, and the foreman stated that unless some stringent measures were adopted the prisoner would be either burnt or scalded to death.—As this was not the prisoner's irst offence, the Bench sentenced him to two months' hard labour. .

Lunt" WEIGHTS AT WIDNES. James Davies, green- grocer, Irwell-street, was summoned to Widnes Petty Ses- sions on Wednesday, to answer a charge of having unjust weights. Superintendent Barker proved that on the 23rd May the defendant had a 21b weight 2 drachms light, a 21b, 5 drachms; 21b, 1 drachm; 21b, 1i drachms ; and three llb , weights each a drachmlight. She was fined 20s and costa: As the defendants promised to have the weights adjusted Supt. Barker did not apply to have them forfeited. Owen, the iecretary, stated that 130 members had been enrolled daring the year, bringing up the total to the maximum of 500 There had been nine appropriations during the year, amounting to £2.200, mak- ing a total of 21 appropriations, amounting to £5,100 since the commencement of the society. The profits on the year's working amounted to £l7O. Messrs. S. Robinson, J. Far- rant,.J. Betney, and Coxon were appointed directors. Mr. T. J. Peters was re-appointed solicitor, and Mr. S. P.S. Strickland skw the horse attached to a cart hi Moor-latie. It was in poor con- dition and was very lame on the hind feet, which were ois- covered to be .• running mater" and emitted a horrible etench. Inspector Wood, who had examined the horse at the police station, gave evidence to this effsct. Edward Doyle, blacksmith in the emoloy of Mr. Thomas, Victoria- road, stated the horse was suffering front " thrueh " w hien was caused through dirty feet. Ech defendant was fined 10s and costs. The father was then charged with being drunk in court on the 27th May. and he was fiaed 55. and costs 65 6cl. Tie Board also wrote in reference' Is Mr Wrie!,t's proposed superannuation grant of £52 per annum, tie.' soey should defer a decision on the matter until the accounts of Mr. Wright, up to the day of his ceasing to 11.,1.1 office, should have been submitted to the district eteiiter and certified by him to he correct. Having received theme letters without comment, the Board proceeded to relief business. BRUTAL ATTACK" ON A RUNCORN CONSTARLE.—At Bun. corn Petty Sesamns on Monday Peter Connally was charged with assaulting P.C. Bason. Shortly after eleven o'clock on Saturday night the constable was walking down Bruns- wick towards his lodgings when he met the prisoner, who inquired what time it was. He told him him twenty past eleven, and remarked that it was time for all honest people to be in bed. As he was in the act of returning the watch to his packet, the prisoner seized him by the legs and threw him en his face with great violence. His face was bruised and cut very badly, and he was stunned for some time. He had always been on friendly terms with the prisoner.—The prisoner alleged that he found the constable on his knees in the street with his face bleeding, and he helped him up as he was drunk.—Superintendent Leah called P.S. Whalley who had seen Bacon at half-past ten, and P.C. Thompson who had seen him at ten minutes past eleven, and they deposed that he was then quite sober, and his face was un- injured.—Tbe Bench fined the prisoner £2, and costs, 14s 101, or in default a month's hard labour. EXCISE PROSECUTION AGAINST A DITTOS MAN.—At the Woniton Potty Sessions, yesterday week, William Thomas, of Halebank. was charged at the instance of Mr. Benjamin Tighe, one of the excise officers, with using a gun on the 11th April last without having a licence.—Mr. Husband appeared for the defendant; and Mr. Heal, who represented the Excise authorities, stated that defendant on the day in question went on some land at Ditton and shot two fowl, the property of John Yates, for which offence be was fined by the Widnes benck.—Mr. Husband admitted the shooting of the fowl, but contended that the defendant, being occu- pier of the land, was entitled under the Act to use a gun without a licence for the purpose of scaring bird?, and sub- mitted that all that he had to do was to prove that the defendant was the occupier of the land.—The magistrates took this view of the case and, nethwithstanding the coo- -1 halation of Mr. Heal that the Act only allowed the gun to be I used to score but not to kill birds, the magistrates dis- missed the Case with costs after hearing evidence of owner- ship. A WIDNES POLICEMAN WOUNDED —Peter O'Loughlin was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly, with assaulting P.C. Gamble, and with doing wilful damage to the officer's clothing. Annie O'Loughlin, his sister, was charged with assaulting ard resisting P.C. Gamble in the execution of his duty. Mr. Knowles defended. About half-past seven on Saturday night Peter was drunk and disorderly in Ann- Street East, and a large crowd assembled. Constables Gamble and Middleton requested him to go away several times, hut. he refused and they took him into custody. Ha struggled violently in order to free himself and struck Gamble several times. His sister then came forward and, It was alleged, threw several stones, one of which struck Gamble on the head. A serious wound was inflicted, and he had lost such a quantity of blood that he had since been off duty. Evidence was given bearing out this account, but Mr Knowles called several witnesses who stated the woman did not throw stones. Mr. Knowles handed up a , ticket to the Bench to show that the woman was going to America in a few days.—The woman was discharged. and Peter was fined 103 and costs for being drunk. £1 and costs for the assault, and 2s 6d compensation for damaging the uniform. or two months' hard labour. PRESENTATION TO Mn. W. E. THORNTON.—On. Wednesday evening the agents of the Refuge Assur- ance Company, Warrington District, presented to Mr. W. E. Thornton, son of Mr. Henry Thornton, dis- trict manager, a handsome massive marble time- piece and a set of beautiful vases, as a token of their esteem and regard. The presentation would have been made on the occasion of Mr. W. E. Thornton's marriage, had not a bereavement suffered by one of the principal members of the presentation commit- tee prevented. A supper was prepared by Mr. Woods, the manager of the Cocoa Rooms, Horse- market-street, and agents from different parts of the district, together with their friends, assembled to do justice to the capital repast. Mr. Cooke of Run- corn, one of the oldest agents of the company present, was moved into the chair. He referred, in terms of high praise, to Mr. W.E. Thornton's integrity and ability. -Mr. Edward Plinston, on being called upon to make the presentation, said he was glad that a good and friendly feeling had always existed be- tween the office and the agents of the Refuge As- surance Company, and gave it as his opinion that the success which the company had obtained, and which he considered unprecedented, was in no small measure due to it. He would give Mr. Thornton, jun., praise for the efforts he had made to bring about this satisfactory state of things. He was sure every agent joined with• him in wishing long life and prosperity to Mr. W. E. Thornton and his worthy wife. Mr. W. E. Thornton suitably thanked the agents for their handsome present. He said he would value it not only for its worth and beauty, but also, and in a greater degree, as a mark of their appreciation. Mr. Henry Thornton, at the request of the Chair- man, addressed a few words to the meeting. He said he was very pleased to meet so many of the agents, and thanked them most heartily for their kindhess to his son. The company, he said, had been singularly successful. None paid its claims more promptly or with less trouble to the members. A programme of a varied kind was then gone through, and short pertinent speeches were given by several gentlemen.

HARD ON S/R RICHARD CROS*L—The London cor- respondent of the Liverpool Daily Yost, writing on Wednesday, says :—" There are many rumours fly- ing about to-day in connection with the crisis, but only two are'absolutely certain. One is that Mr. , Gladstone will decline to make any effort to recon- struct the Ministry, and the other that Lord Salis- bury is ready to take office if called upon. He will find, ready-made, several Administrations. Of course the list published merely points to what in various quarters appears probable. I have met to- day several Conservatives who are certain to fill some office in the new Ministry, and heard one or , two things which.are accepted as probable in the best informed Conservative circles. It is not true that Sir Baliol Brett is to have the Woolsack; Sir Hardinge Giffard claims it as his right, and will I certainly get it. This leaves two vacancies for law ' officers, which will probably be filled by Mr. Clarke and Mr. Gorst. Sir M. Hicks-Beach hankers after the Home office; Mr. W. H. Smith will be made a peer; and Sir Richard Cross, whose failure has long been acknowledged, will be provided for in the same convenient asylum." ALLBGED FriAtrnuLErrr RAILRR.—At the Borough Court, yesterday, a watch .repairer named George Mills, of Admiral-street, Warrington, was charged that he, being bailee of a silver lever watch, the property of Jesse Leach, Okell-street, Runcorn, did commit the same to his own use. The prosecutor, as stated by Chief Constable Hunt, is a carrier be- tween Runcorn and Warrington, and between the 23rd and 30th May three watches were entrusted by him to prisoner for repair, having been handed to him (prosecutor) by different people for that ob- ject. On the 30th May he entrusted his own watch to prisoner to clean and repair. Not regaining it on several applications he demanded it, cleaned or not, but failed to get it. In consequence he made inquiries at a pawnshop; and found that the same watch had there been , pawned by a person giving the name of the prisoner. Further inquiries revealed the fact that the other watches had been pawned at another shop, and, the Chief Constable added, he , had reason to believe that a watch had been pawned that had been given , for .repairs to prisoner by a lady. In answer to the Bench prosecutor said that , through previous transactions he knew prisoner to . be a watch repairer. Prisoner, who said he pre- I ferred to be ;tned by a jury, was remanded for in- quiries. LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT FOOTBALL ASSOCIA- TION: ANNUAL AIRETING.—The annual meeting of the Liverpool and District Football Association, em- bracing clubs in the St. Helens, Warrington, Earls- town, and Golbonie districts was held at the Nep- tune Hotel, Liverpool, on , Thursday week. The Earlstown Club (holders of the Challenge Cup) were represented by Messrs. P. Bostic and W. Moses; Hayclock Temperance by Messrs. G. 11. Hunt and T. Wedgwood; Earlestown Wanderers by Messrs. T. Champion and Wilson; Hay-dock' St. James's by Messrs. T. Harrison and Bailey. Amongst the other clubs represented were Everton, Bootle, Stanley Ramblers, Cambrian,. St. Peter's, St. Mary's, &c. Mr. A. B. Hull (chairman of the association) presided. After the minutes of the last meeting had been read and confirmed, Mr. E. Stewart-Brown (Ramblers), as one of the auditors, read the balance sheet. The total receipts amounted to £2OB 2s sd, leaving a balance of £6B 2s lid in Parr's Bank. Mr. Stewart- Brown thought the figures spoke for themselves-- • (hear, hear)—and moved the adoption of the balance sheet. Mr. Heard (Bootle) seconded the motion. which was unanimously carried. Mr. T. Evans : (Everton) moved that seeing the association had a I good balance, that the amounts subscribed by the different clubs towards the Challenge Cup be re- funded, and Mr. Stewart-Brciwn (Ramblers) seconded . the proposition. As an amendment Mr. P. Hastie (Earlestown) proposed that the association place , such amounts to the credit of the local charities. 4 This was seconded by Mr. Lamont (St. Peter's), and I carried by twelve votes to eight. Mr. Sloan (Bootle). then moved a further amendment that the money be retained by the association, which was lost by 13 to 12 votes. Mr. R. E. Lythgoe (the honorary secre- tary) next read the annual report, showing the pro- gress of the association, which was considered highly satisfactory, and passed. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the committee, chairman, treasurer, , and 'secretary for their services during the past year, after which the president, vice-presidents, and patrons were re-elected. Mr. E. S. Brown (Ram- blers) was nominated as treasurer, but as he declined to stand Mr. T. Evans (Everton) was unanimously appointed. Mr. R. E. Lythgee was Unanimously re- elected honorary secretary. The election of commit- tee then took place. This was the principal business, and the meeting shortly afterwards con- cluded.

The gas and water revenue accounts had been submitted and showed a profit of £372 lOs 101 on gas, and £3,043 16s 4d en Gasket' moved the confirmation of the minutes, and ob- served that the profit on gas ought to be about £250 more than stated in the minutes.
