The Highway Committee's minutes contained a recom- mendation that Mrs. Hunt be paid 53. per yard for 110 square yards of land, laid to Albert-road some years age. It was also recommended that no epposition lee offered by the Board to the cloning of West Bank-street from Hutchin- son-street to Marsh-street, upon T. Bolton and Sons enter- ing into an agreement to widen Marsh-street as suggested; to open West Batik-street, if that street should be required for the approach to any bridge which may be erected for the purpose of doing away with Waterloo-road level crow. ing ; to protect the Board's sewer ; and other conditions.— Mr. Carey moved, and Mr. Houghton seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Hayes asked for an explanation of the remark in the Surveyor's report that Messrs. Sayee and , Randle had commenced their main sewer contract. —Mr. Brown said be understood a new-sewer had been put in from Anderson's-corner along Lugsdale-road, in the direction of I Ann-street, and he asked if it would be capable of draining the cellars in that neighbourhood.—Mr. Carer, in reply to Mr. Heyes, said as a new member he might not be aware of the unfortunate catastrophe that had taken place with re- gard to this sewer. Part of the sewer constructed by Jeffreys bad given way, and as far as could be estimated about 40 yards would have to be reconstructed. In addition to that, the arbitration that took place between the Board ' and Hutchinson's Trustees 801110 time ago, as to alleged damage done by Mr. Jeffreys to Hutchinson's sewer, had the result that the Board had to repair a length of that sewer at their own expense. It was this work that was now being done by Messrs. Seyce and Randle. The sewer referred to by Mr. Brown was only being cleaned out, but the Suryeyor had not brought the matter before the committee in any way.—Mr. Brown said he should like to sea the Surveyor whether it was likely that whenever there was a little more rain than ordinary, the places in Lugsdale-road would be flooded, same as they were on Monday. lie understood that when the brook was enclosed, and the new road made, that these floods would stop. The flood on Monday had been a very serious matter to his firm, as the works had to be stopped.—Mr. Carey said floods depended upon the state of Bower's Brook. He hoped that when the Board could afford it, that the main sewer would be constructed to Oxford-at., , which would then drain all the low-lying land. Until thee they would be subject to occasional floods. The committee did their best to keep the brook clean. Replying to a ques- tion by Dr. O'Keeffe as to the stoppage of \Vat Bank-streete Mr. Carey said this matter had had the anxious considera- ,tion of the committee since he had the honour of being chairman, and they had had many interviews with Messrs. Bolton and with some of the property owners in the district. The arrangement that Messrs. Bolton were willing to enter into was of such a character that the Board would have no cause for complaint, and in fact the committee thought it would confer a public benefit. That being the case, the committee had no reason on behalf of the public to oppose the stoppage of the rreet. As far as they understood the managers of the schools in Hutchinson-street were satisfied with the arrangement that had been made, and bad de- clined to have Peel-street stopped up in order that they might have a larger play ground.—Dr. O'Keeffe stated that the managers did not agree to the closing of West Bank. Street, bat were on the contrary most decidedly against such a course. He ridiculed the idea of widening March-street, which was scarcely inhabited, and alleged that it was being done for the benefit of tne Atlas Chemical Works and the Mersey Copper Works. He asked why not widen it the whole distance to Waterloe-road. The proposed arrange- ment was one of the most glaring pieces of absurdity that could be placed before gentlemen of intelligence, and who- ever was the author, he deserved a leather medal. The in- definiteness of the arrangement was sufficient to condemn the whole affair. It was like buying a pig in a poke. He moved that the consideration of the matter be adjourned until the next meeting.—Mr. Carey pointed out that a special meeting would have to be called to rescind a former resolution, and discuss the details of the arrangement. —Mr. Sadler seconded the amendment —Mr. Brown said not one per cent of the workmen used the street, and he thought the Board competent to deal with the matter that day.—The amendment was lost by eight votes to four.—Dr. O'Keeffe hatimated that he should oppose the closing of the street at the Quarter Sessions.—Mr. Carey replied that it was open to any ratepayer to do so, The minutes of the Health Committee contained the report of the Medical Officer of Health, which stated that during May there were 94 births and 31 deaths representing a rate of 4177 and 13.77 per 1,000 respectively. Nine deaths oc- curred amongst children under one year, and four between one and five years. The committee recommended that the present system of nightsoil work be continued, and that tenders he invited for the removal of nightsoil for one, two, or three years —The agreement for the three acres of land for site for infectious diseases hospital and other land for widening roads, from the Trustees of Legh estate, was submitted, and it was recommended that it be sealed. —Plan of suggested administrative buildings, estimated to submitted, only one-half to be built at present. I mended that it be approved.—The Market In- esptese was tctlorl;sornCl, reported that the receipts for the month amounted to £53 Sc 10d, being an increase of £2l 5s 7d on the correse pending period last year.—ln moving the adoption of the minutes, Dr. O'Keeffe referred with gratification to the low death rate, and said it was cause for satisfaction that dur- ing the five months of the present year the average death rate was only 16,per thousand. There bad been no cases of infectious disease during the past month. It bad been re- ported that there was a case of smallpox, but this was un- true. The committee had made an iaspecion of the tows, and the sanitary condition was in a satisfactory state. There were several cases of smallpox in Gersten in the best locali- ties, and it was possible, considering the intercourse be- tween the two towns, that the disease might be imported into Widnes, and it was important that the plans of the Infections Diseases Hospital should be proceeded with with- out delay. He referred in terms of warm praise to the hospital arrangements at Runcorn, and to the kindness he had received at the bands of Mr. W. Handley when on. visit to that institation.—The minutes were seconded and adopted, and it was decided that the plans for the hospital should be discussed at the special meeting,

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL .BILL.—A public meeting in support of the Ship Canal Bill now be- fore Parliament was held on Saturday afternoon in the Town Hall at Eccles. The meeting was well attended, and presided over by Mr. Richard James, Ilimston. Mr. John Pearson movedthat the meeting thank Mr. Daniel Adamson and his committee for their services in connection with the scheme, and 'pledge itself to assist them to the utmost of their power in carrying the bill to a successful issue.— The motion was seconded by Mr. Charles Entwistle, and was unanimously adopted.—ln acknowledging the compliment, Mr. Daniel Adamson'expressed the conviction that the Manchester Ship Canal was wan- ted not only by Manchester and England, but by the whole world. They had stilt a formidable battle to fight, but he was hopeful of success. The Corn-1 mittee of Selection of the House of Commons met on Tuesday, under the presidency of Sir John Mow- bray, for the purpose of appointing the Select Com- mittee on the Ship Canal Bill. Mr. W. E. Forster, the senior member for Bradford, was selected as chairman. The other members chosen being Lord Eustace Cecil, the junior member for West Essex ; Mr. Dalrymple, the junior member .for Buteshire ; and Mr. W. Fowler, the senior member for the borough of Cambridge. It was decided that the Committee should meet to consider the Bill on Mon- day next, at 12 o'clock.—A petition against the canal scheme that has been drawn up by the Liverpool Steamship Owners Association points out that there would be both danger and delay in passing through the canal, that the danger would cause heavier in- surance charges both on ship and cargo, and that the delay would necessarily involve additions to freight to cover the additional wages and interest i on the cost of the vessel, which n many cases amounts to as much as £lOO per day.—The Bootle Town Council on Wednesday night unanimously re- solved by caunsel and petition to oppose the Manches- ter Ship Canal Bill.lt was urged in favour of the pro-. pose/ that indications of the bill passing the House of Lords were so strong that the Corporation did not think it worth while to oppose it when before the Select Committee of their lordships, but when it came before the Committee of the House of Com- mons it should be opposed as strongly as possible. Bootle was equally interested with Liverpool iii the port's prosperity, And when the fight came they would be prepared to take part in it.—On Thursday objections by the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill to the locus stanfei of several petitioners were considered by the Come of Referees. Dr. O'Reeffe drew the attention of the Board to the fact that the water of a brook that flowed near Netherlay pump- ing station was much contaminated bye sewage farm in the neighbourhood. A scientik chemist belonging to Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co., had analysed the water, and he pronounced it to be one of the worst specimens he had ever seen or tested. It pas simply liquid sewage runner, and. he asked most respectfully that the Gas and Water would deal with the matter.—Mr. Gaskell observed that the Water Committee were aware of the impurity,. and woukt deal with it.

THB ANNUAL INSPECTION. Dr. O'Keeffe moved, and Mr. Houghton seconded, that the annual inspection be held on Thursday, the 25th inst.— Mr. Gaskell moved,and Mr. Dutton secon,Ted an amendment that the inspection be not held. Both gentlemen were of opinion it were unnecessary.—The amendment was carzied by 7 votes to 5.

ASSAULT ON A WlFE.—Henry Clare, who is in employ of the Corporation, was charged with aasaulting his wife, to whom he had been married eighteen months, on the 3rd Inst., and was bound over to be of good behaviour. MISCHLLANEOUS,—kndrew Dunn, for being drunk in San- key-street, on the previous evening, was fined 5s and costs, and Patrick Fallon, for drunkenness, in Dial-street, on the ,previous evening, was similarly fined.—Frank Hall and William Howard were each fined 7s 6d, including costs, for stone throwing.—John Leonard, charged with begging in Bridge-street, on Saturday evening, was dismissed with a reprimand; and James Smith, for begging in Froghall-lane OR Silndhy, was ordered to pay is, the lock-up fee. dians.—We have taken stepg-to have the costs ofthe Guar- dians taxed, but are met with the difficulty that the Registrar of the Court says that having regard to the scale of charges by which he is now guided, and section 35 of 19 and 20 Vic., c. 108, he is not authorised to allow any other charges than those he has already allowed on taxation as against the Commissioners, z e., that costs as between party and party and as between solicitor and client are practically the same under the scale by which he has to go, unless the client has agreed in writing to pay anything besides what is sanctioned by the scale. We showed him the resolution of the Board instructing us to retain counsel and do all that was necessary to have the case fought out, but he does not consider that such resolutions constitute an agreement in writing to pay anything beyond the scale allowances to counsel and solicitor. We cannot say that the registrar is wrong as to his construction of the Act, and , scale costs are seldom taxed as between solicitors and client, and therefore the question does not often arise. In this case, however, I was desirdus of having the bill taxed, as I myself am a Guardian, and only desire to have to have what 'was allowed on taxation as between solicitor and client. On taxation, as against the Commissioners, I only got allowed a comparatively small portion of counsel's fees actually paid by me. The total amount allowed was £29 25.; our total payments out of pocket was £2l 125., so that the amount allowed for all our time and trouble is £7 10s. I think the best way is to send you the bill in the ordinary way, to be dealt with as other bills are usually dealt with, and whatever the Guardians think proper to allow, whether the whole or a part, I shall be satisfied therewith, as I took up the case more for fighting for the principle involved than with a view to my own personal gain in the matter. You had better lay the bill, with this letter, before the Guar- dians, or the committee who usually deal with accounts. The general committee of the National Liberal Club has passed a resolution declaring that the disqualification of electors by the receipt of medical relief ought to he re- moved by legislation during the present Parliament. A fire occurred on Wednesday in Whitechapel, London, and on its being extinguished it was found that one of the tenants, Mrs. Roach, was 80 severely burned that she had to be taken to the hospital, whilst her child, two years old, was suffocated.

The Marquis of Lorne attended the annual meeting of the Yorkshire Union of Mechanics' Institutes, held on Wed- nesday at York, and in the afternoon officiated at the open- ing of the new building of the York Institute of Literature, Art, and Science.

The annual meeting of the English Church Union was held in London on Wednesday under the presidency of the Hon. C. L. Wood. Reference was made both in the Chair- man's speech and the report of tha Executive to the "revi- val of peraecution "in Liverpool. DASTARDLY 017TRAGE.—MTS. Hamill, a widow, living at Market-hill, near Newry, had her home maliciously set on fire early on Monday morning. Some men entered the pre- mises and rescued her at the risk of their lives, but the house and contents were entirely destroyed. CHILD MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. On Mon- day, at Wolverhampton, Mrs Ann Jones threw her child into the Wingpath Canal, and then jumped in herself. The woman was rescued in an exhausted condition, bat the child was drowned. Domestic trouble is said to be the cause of the act.

HE EVOLUTIONARY SQUADRON. The evolutionary squadron, under Admiral Hornby, sailed from Portland, on Tuesday for Bantry Bay in fine weather. Thirteen laage vessels assembled. Admiral Hornby expects to meet off Bishops Light the Conquest, Mariner, Racer, and Mercury. Other vessels will join the squadron at Bantry, making a total of 28 vessels and eight, torpedo boats. The inflexible will not join the squadron, the future movements of which are not fixed, nor is the date of its return definitely ar- ranged. The seem:lL...mid meeting for -le season in con- nection with the Liverpool Field Naturalists Club was held at Newton• and Winwick on Saturday. Upwards of, seventy members and friends assembledl at Lime-street Station, and proceeded to Newton Bridge. Here they were met by the Rev. J. Car- son, curate of Winwick, who -obligingly acted as guide, and Mr. W. Haskell, of Newton-le-Willows. By the kind permission of Mr. Stone, the walk com- menced up the drive of Newton Park. After a visit to the billiard-room, to see some fine specimens of old oak carving, the party were conducted by the, Messrs. Stone through the garden, and then, by tt,te I fine kennels, into the fields as far as Hermit,ave L Glen, a beautifully wooded dell with a blaze of. bells on the banks below. The next point w•as Wan- wick Cottage, a most picturesque Structuro„ covered with ivy, tenanted by an owl, and a gr.eed, variety of natural history creations. Mr:Wor-Alley, 'who re- sides there, courteously led the cl-Ab th h his charming grounds, and accompanic4 them to Win- wick Church and Hall. Enterin2 the church, Mr. Carson called attention to 0-40 monuments and numerous bronzes, one represeAting Sir Peter Leigh, who became a priest after 'ening- a, crusader. The altar cloth and carpet werfa. beautifully worked by Lady Eleanor, wife of Ca.aon Hopwood, rector, after she was seventy. Their golden wedding is to be celebrated with liTeat Mat on the 11th June. The marriage register 'was also inspected, the first entry being in 1563. Mr. Worley being a well-known local antiquarian, then gave an interesting histori- cal description of the church. Its foundation dates back from remote antiquity, the Norman-pillars on the north side being undoubtedly older than the 'fine tower and spire, which were built about 1350. The earliest record is the remains of a stone cross with Runic characters, now in the churchyard, sup- posed to be a preaching station of some early mis- sionary of the seventh or eighth century. The church is dedicated to St. Oswald, also king of Wordan- hymbrorum, according toßede killed in battle; ac- cording to Nennius at the battle of Cocboy by the ediabolical acts of Ponda. Ile was a saint of great reputation, as Oswestry and other places lay claim to him. On the west front of the tower is carved an image of a pig with n bell round its neck. Popu- lar tradition calls it a stone, and says the bearer carried it up every night from some other spot to indicate the site for the church. Mr. Worsley has incontestibly proved from his researches in numer- ous old churches that a hog with a bell round its neck was the recognised symbol of St. Anthony. He was patron of church towers and bells, and his statue once, no doubt, occupied the now empty niche over the pig. St. Anthony is often represen- ted as standing on a hog, typifying his victory over sensuality. It is a singular fact that swine belong- ing to the Abbot of St. Anthony in the twelfth cen- tury were permitted to range unmolested in the streets of Paris and London if they had bells round their necks. Winwick Hall stands in a well-wooded park, with a charming shady walk all round t. Henry the Seventh and James the First rested in the original house on their way to Lathom. .War- rington Bridge was built for the accommodation of Henry. The way back crossed "Winwick Pass" and Gallows Croft, the scene of Cromwell's victory over the Duke of Hamilton, and the Reformatory Farm School, which want of time prevented, a visit by the party. Tea was provided by the club caterer (Mr. Griffiths) in the Town Hall, Newton, after which a stroll through thlonel McCorquodale's beautiful grounds, and a row on Newton Mere to Mr. Pearson's, of Golborne Park, terminated the pro- ceedings of a most enjoyable day. The lovely vivid green of the early foliage and the abundance of flower on hawthorn, rhododendrons, &c*, combined to lend additional charm to the natural beauties of this rural district. The order prize was taken. by Miss Moss, with five specimens. The botanical enigma was solved by Mrs J. Vicars, Misses E. Tnr- mean and E. Adams, Messrs. J. Vicars andE. Davies, the plant being furula campestris. The .bouquet prize was taken by Miss M. Turmeau. Some inter- esting plants were also found by botanists at the head of the mere.

A PECULIAR WAY OF PAYING DEBTS.—In this case Anti Maddock sued John Higgins for the recovery of cer- tain articles of clothing of the value of £2 12e.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. P. Davies for the defence.—lt appeared from Mr. Browne' s opening statement that on Easter Monday the plaintiff, who is a provision dealer living in Glasshouse-row, lent the defendant's wife some articles of clothing. Mrs. Higgins said that her hus- band was unable to work, and the goods were lent to her for the purpose of pawning in order to raise some money. As defendant's wife declined to give the articles up, this action was taken to recover them.—His Honour said he would amend the plaint, and make defendant's wife the de- fendant.—Mrs. Higgins, in giving evidence, said she lived at Glasshouse-row, and was the wife of John Higgins, who was a forge labourer employed at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.'s works. On three occasions Mts. Maddock brought articles of elothing to her to pawn, as she (witness) had not sufficient to pay.for provisions she had obtained from the plaintiff. She redeemed the articles on two occasions, and paid off a portion of the debts she had incurred with plaintiff.—His Honour gave a verdict tot £2, which would Pe reduced tif Is, if the articles were redeemed within a fortnight. The judgment would be against the separate estate of the wife.

A DISPUTE ABOUT COTTAGE BUILDING.—WM. FUITRISS, shopkeeper, in Lyttgoes-lane, claimed from Robert Priddon, bricklayer, £2 34 4d, balance owing for work left unfinished by defendant in the erection of six cottages in a street off Stony-lane. A counter claim was put in by the defend- ant for £2 2s 63 for extra work done by him.—Mr. Years- ley represented the defendant —The plaintiff contended that the defendant, who had undertaken to erect these cottages, had left unfinished certain internal fittings, and also the staircase walls, which were to be of brick. In con- sequence of this he bad other, workmen to engage to com- plete the work.—Defendant, on the other hand, maintained that the staircase walls were shown on the plan to be of wood.—Judgment was given for 13s 4cl on the plaintiff's claim, and for 15s on the counter-claim. A COMPMCATED LOAN CASE.—JOBepb Wadsworth and Co. brought an action against James Love 3, his wife Sarah Ann Lovett (formerly Sarah Ann Blundell), and Thomas Whitley, for the recovery of a loan.—Mr. Jenkins said he appeared on behalf of the plaintiffs and the guarantor, Thomas Wbitley.—His Honour: You cannot appear on behalf of them both,—Mr. Jenkina : Those are my in- structions.—His Honour: That may be, but you cannot appear for them both.—Mr. Jenkins said he would, there- fore, confiee his remarks for the plaintiff. He then pro- ceeded to say that that case was brought to recover a balance of £6 3s, being £3 15a balance of principal and £2 8s for interest. It appeared, he said, that a Mrs. Blundell, who was then a widow, borrowed 5.5 from this Loan Com- pany on the 19th July, 1880. Subsequently in August, 1883, she married the defendant Lovett, and en the 24th July. 1884, she died. Subsequently Mrs. Lovett, as repre- senting her late husband, Mr. Blundell, became entitled to a share of moneys left under the will of a grandfather of Mr. Blundell. The defendant Jas. Lovett took the share to which Mrs. Blundell was entitled, and received that sum at the offices of Messrs. Kenyon and Tyrer, Liverpool. A Mrs. Jones, who was the sister of the late Mrs. Blundell, would prove, as she was present, that the defendant Lovett received that share.—His Honour said that did not make Lovett liable.—Mr. Jenkins contended that Lovett was liable in whatever capacity he received the assets.—His Honour did not think that. Lovett only received what he was entitled to, and the money was only assets so long as it was in the bonds of an administrator —Mr. Jenkins said he contended that Lovett was administrator.—Mr. Lovett said he would swear he was not. He repudiated any lia- bility, and he looked upon it as a fraud to sty that the signature to the note was that of Sarah Ann Blundell.— Some evidence having been given, his Honour gave a ver- dict for the plaintiff so far as Whitley was concerned; and with regard to Lovett's liability, adjourned the case in order that evidence as to administration might be ob- tained.

Ralph Fenwick was elected provident, and Mr. Thomas Lawrence vice-president for the errtning year. A conference of representatives of the coffee-house indus- try was opened on Wednesday in Liverpool, under the presidency of the Rev. Charles (lomat, who stated that the movement, which was exercising so greet and beneficial an influence upon the working classes, bad its origin as a national organisation in that city. POISONED THROUGH EATING SANDWICHES.—EmiIy Chap PIM, aged 17, daughter of a Harrowgate draper, died on Monday, it is alleged, through eating vanilla sandwiches purchased in Leeds. Mrs Chappel and her youngest chil- dren, Annie and Charles, also became ill after partaking of the sandwiches. The latter soon recovered, but the others remain in a dangerous state. THE OPIUM TRADE.--At the annual meeting in London on Thursday of the Society for the Suppression of the Opium Traffic a resolution was passed expressing the earnest hope that the agreement with China would keep the way open for the ultimate suppression of the vice of opium eating, and urging the Viceroy of India to restrict the growth of the poppy to the extent required for medicinal purposes. THE HULL CHILD MURDER.--At Hull Police Court, on Thursday, a young girl named Isabella Hewson was charged with the murder other illegitimate child by banging it. On her brother being called she became terribly excited, shrieked out the name of her child, and went into several fits. She was so violent that two female warders and several officers had to hold her. The hearing of the case had te be suspended. On Tuesday, in the Appeal Court, the Attorney- General informed their lordships that Mr. Adam's actions against Hon. B. Coleridge and Lord Coleridge bad been eettled to the mutual satisfaction of both parties. The ques- tion of compensation would be referred to a third party, who had consented to arbitrate. All imputations were with- drawn. With regard to the Hon. Mildred Coleridge, she would be reinstited in the position she occupied before the litigation, and Lord Coleridge would settle £6OO a year on her.

THE PRINCE OF WALES AND CHARLES DARWlN.—Pro- lessor Huxley, on Tuesday, unveiled the statue of Charles Darwin in the Natural History Museum, South Kensington, In the presence of a large assembly, including the Prince of Wales, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Lords Sherbrooke and Houghton, Canon Farrar, Herbert Spencer, Robert Browning, and many other distinguished persons. The Prince of Wales, accepting the statue on behalf of the British Museum, said they willingly afsigned an honourable place to the statue of a great Englishman who had exerted so vast an influence upon the progress of natural knowledge. FROM THE LAND'S END TO Joule O'GROAT'S ON A BICY- CLE.—Mr. E. Oxborrow, of the St. Jbhn's Bicycle Club, who started from the Land's End on a Facile machine at 3-45 cm. on Monday week, arrived at John O'Groat's at 2-55 a.m. last Monday. After passing Dingwall, through mis- direction he went 20 miles out of his wa, and had to re- trace Ms steps. On resuming he had covered 19 miles,when the rim of his wheel broke in three places. He then tele- graphed to Inverness for another [machine, which was sent on by train, and he proceeded across Mickle Ferry, through Golspie and Hemsdale to Wick, and from there to the ead of his journey. ARRIVAL OF SIR PETER LUMSDEN.—Sir Peter Lumsden arrived in London on Saturday evening, and met with a most enthusiastic reception from an immense crowd as- sembled to meet him,which included no fewer than three fiebi marshals of the British army, together with other officers, members of Parliament, and persons of distinction. As the mail train from the Centinent steamed into Charing Cross Station at six o'clock there was immense cheering upon the appearance of the gallant general at the window of a saloon carriage, in company with Lady Lumsden, his brother, Sir Henry and Lady Harry Lumsden, and Mr. Condi° Stephen, who had gone to Paris to meet him. Among the many who personally congratulated Sir P. Lumsden was Sir Richard Cross, M P. DOUBLE MURDER BE A MOTHER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. —Margaret Hibbert, of Fernleaf-street, Moss Side, was brought before the magistrates at the County Police Court, Manchester, on Saturday, and she cried bitterly during the proceedings, and seemed to be greatly prostrated. The cir- cumstances of the case were briefly gone into, and a remand granted for a week. In the afternoon an inquest was held upon the bodies of the children. No particulars were made known beyond those published in our Saturday's issue. Dr Cartaael gave it as his opinion that Mrs Hibbert was suffer- ing from melancholia.—The Coroner told the jury that they had not to consider whether the prisoner was same or insane when she committed the murder.--A verdict of " Wilful murder" against Mrs Hibbert waireturned. THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.—Her Majesty's birthday was officially celebrated on Saturday. The ceremony of troop- ing the colours took place on Saturday,en the Horse Guards' Parade, in the presence of the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke of Cambridge, and the Duke of Edinburgh. The usual evolutions were strictly carried out in spite of heavy and centinuous rain, Which totally spoiled the effect of this usually imposing spectacle. In the evening the customary banquets were given by the Ministers and high officers of State. The Prince of Wales and Prince Albert Victor dined with Mr. Gladstone, and the Duke of Edin- burgh with the First Lord of the Admiralty, The Marquis of Hartington gave a State dinner at Devonshire House, among the guests being H.R.H. the Duca of Cambridge. A SAD AFFAIR.—At Hampton, on Monday, Victor E. Wicks, 16 years of age, was charged with causing the death of his brother, Prince G. Wicks, 18. on Sunday both young men went for a walk, the prisoner haying in his hand a bunch of flowers, which he intended to present to a young lady at Shepperton, whither he was going. The deceased was desirous of possessing some of the flowers, and kept knocking them with his stick and threatening the prisoner. The latter, it is alleged, struck the defendant with a penknife in the region of the heart, inflicting a punctured wound , about two inches deep, from the effects of which the de- ceased died in a few minutes. The prisoner, not thieking that he had hurt his brother mortally, proceeded on his journey to Shepperton, where he was arrested later in the day. The prisoner was remanded. EXPLOSION ON BOARD IL Wen Sere. On Monday morning, about 1,200 tons of coal had been stowed on board the Inflexible by a steam collier and lighter, when explo- sions occurred, injuring 13 men. In most cases the injuries are of a superficial character, but three were so badly burnt that they had to be removed to Hasler Hospital. On Sun- day night, when the Metropolitan police made their usual search of the ship, they found the stoke hole was shut and the bunkers covered, thus excluding the possibility of ven- tilation. Coleman, the chief stoker of the party, states that there was a large flame and but a slight report. He attri- butes the explosion to the naked light being sent down before the bunkers had been cleared of gas. He and the other men injured say the bunker lids should have been re- moved the previous night. An inquiry will be held into the cause of the accident. None of the men injured belong to the Royal Navy, as they were employed by the codling steamers alongside the Inflexible. PRINCEss BEATRICE'S WEDDING CAKE.-'--The following is a description of the wedding cake made to the order of Kentish ladies by Messrs. Buszard, of Oxford-street, Lon- don, for Her Royal Highness Princess Beatrice :—lt repre- sents three cakes, one-above the other, and the plateau upon which it rests, and surrounding the lower cake, is a wreath of lilies, white, interspersed with ivy, emblematic of purity, sweetness, and friendship. Surrounding the lowest cake are large skeleton shields, bearing on enclosed shields the coat of arms of the Princess Beatrice and Prince Henry of Bat- tenberg, interspersed with passion flowers. Surrounding the second cake are jessamine, and round the second and third cakes are passion flowers, ivy, and roses. OR the top cake are cupids and a large vase containing an immense ' bouquet composed of a variety of emblematic flowers. The cake weighs about 4cwt., and the floral decorations are all ' modelled entirely of sugar. It will be pieced on a massive gold stand, which is being specially made and designed for ' the occasion. THE COLLISION WITH THE CITY OF ROME —22 LINES LOST.—Particulars have been received of the accident off the coast of Newfoundland, when the steamer City of Rome I ran down, the French fishing barque George Cl Jeanne. The l fishing vessel foundered immediately, carrying with her 22 hands, all of whom perished. It appears that the steamer was speeding through a dense fog on the banks of New- foundland on the afternoon of May 25th at the rate of from ' 14 to 17 knots, with the whistle sounding every half min- ute. Captain Munro was on the bridge when, at 430, the ' lookout discovered the outlines of a vessel on the edge of the fog directly ahead. The sails of this vessel were furltd, and she was apparently at anchor. "Sail ahead," cried the lookout, and Captain Munroe instantly ordered the engines to be reversed. It was too late to clear the strange vessel, and through the fog four figures were seen to rush forward on her deck uttering a wild cry which will not soon be forgotten by those who beard it. In another instant the , ' City of Rome struck the barque, her sharp iron bow meet- ing the side of the doomed vessel. The crash of wood and the wild clamour of human voices filled the air, but not for long. In less than half a minute the wrecked vessel hat sunk, and four men were seen floating in the icy water clinging to the wreckage. Two lifeboat, were quickly drop- ped into the water and several lifebuoys were tossed over- board. By these means two men were drawn aboard almost exhausted. All the men of the barque were married. The passengers of the City of Rome, who were deeply moved by the disaster, made a collection for their benefit. Perineum. COMMITTEE.—The monthly meeting of the Go!borne Parochial Committee was held on Wednesday afternoon in Messrs. It. Evans and Co.'s office. The follow- ing members were present :—Messrs. W. Mitchell (chair- man), Taylor, Lawton, Arnott, T. Mitchell, Pierpoint, Foams, Garton, Yates, Grimke, and the Surveyor.—The Surveyor read the minutes of the last meeting, which were ' confirmed.—Messrs. Walton's tender for 4in. flags was ac- cepted out of a number placed before the Committee.—The Surveyor reported that the Abram footpath question had been brought before the Abram Local Board and the clerk had undertaken to attend to the matter.—An important question respecting the future water supply for the township of Golborne was introduced by the Surveyor, who said he had, as requested by Mr. Grimke, taken levels, F.m., to ascer- tain whether it was advisable to take means of procuring water from Liverpool mains at Stubshaw Cross, near Ashton- in-Makerfield, in view of the probable scarcity of water at present derived from the Ince waterworks. The surveyor said he was of opinion that the scheme was feasible, and the Committee were in favour of the proposed undertaking if arrangements could be made at a satisfactory price. The consumption of water for the previous four weeks was re ported by the surveyor as six hundred and ninety-eight thousand gallons. In consequence of a defective street gas meter the township gas account was left over for the special consideration of the Lighting Committee.—There was no further business of importance before the meeting.

THE ROSE QUEEN AT LOWTON. The crowning of the rose queen took place under most favourable circumstances at Lowton, on Saturday. The district was gaily decorated with flags, bunting, &c., there being few cottages where some attempt bad not been made at outward decoration. Upwards of 500 children assembled on the cricket ground at half-past one, a grand procession, accompanied by three bands of music, being formed half an hour later. The great attraction was the " Queen," Miss Elizabeth Houghton, a pretty girl of ten, who wore a dress of white satin, appropriately trimmed, and veil to match. She occupied an open carriage drawn by a couple of "greys," and was accompanied by her crown bearer, Miss Annie Ashton, aged seven. "Her Majesty !' was attended by pages in handsome costume, the whole "get up" being stately. Amongst the characters taking part in the proces- sion were flower girls, gleaners, milk-maids, weavers, lady archers, 80-peeps, girls representing the seasons, old men and old women (smoking long clays and wearing spectacles), the old woman that lived in a shoe, Welsh women, fish women, gipsies, &c, The characters taken by the boys in- cluded sailors, soldiers, bakers, butchers, joiners, bricklayers, footballers, smiths, strikers, stone-masons, and slaters, each carrying implements indicative of their trade or profession. The Quen's carriage was preceded by a sword-bearer, sceptre-bearer, and the mimic "Archbishop." These all wore costumes specially prepared for the occasion, the lat- ter being dressed as archbishop of Canterbury. After para- ding the district an adjournment was made to a field, where a throne had been erected, a rose pole pro- vided, together with complete arrangements for carrying Out the subsequent proceedings. The coronation was en- trusted to the "archbishop " (Mr Douglas Berwick), and was ably carried out, as were also the duties of the atten- dants. The bands struck up the National Anthem, and hearty cheers were raised by the children. The rose-pole dancing and the plaiting of the ribbons were most taste- fully executed by thirty two prettily dressed maidens, under the able direction of Mr. T. Berwick, of the Grove, Lowton. A tug-o'-war and other amusements followed. About 5,000 persons were present, who frequently testified to the satis- faction the proceedings afforded them. The arrangements were carried out by a committee, with Mr. W. H. Arnott as chairman and Mr. J. Bromley, as secretary. Mr. C. E. Arnott and Mr. Berwick officiated as M.C.'s. The weather was delightfully fine, and the undertaking was a decided success.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, TLIIIRSDA.T. If on this day last week anyone had prophesied that within five days Mr. Gladstone and his Government would have resigned office, and that Lord Salisbury would have kis foot already upon the steps of the Treasury, he would have been regarded as mad. It seemed last week that after * stormy career the Government bad got into smooth waters, where they would remain till the end of things, dis- turbed only by a passing storm in the matter of the Coer- cion Bill. The eighth vote of censure had passed over them harmlessly, and though opposition was threatened on the Budget Bill, it did not appear to have much reality about it. Whatever anxiety may have been felt in view of Sir Michael Hicks-Beach's amendment when it was placed upon the paper, had been removed by the concession made by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The complaint was that he had unduly taxed beer and spirits. The additional impost on beer was really infinitesi- maL An extra shilling on thirty-six gallons would hurt nobody and could not possibly reach the poor man and his modest "dinner pint." The additional two shillings a gal- lon to spirits was a more tangible thing. But Mr. Childers had met this objection by reducing it to one half. The Budget when originally proposed, though not enthusiasti- cally welcomed, as budgets which impose additional taxa- tion are not likely to be, had been on the whole well re- ceived, as a fair compromise with necessity. This lessened charge on spirits would ease its way, and the threatened op- position under the leadership of Sir M. H. Beach was little talked of. It was the same all through the debate. Members, though they crowded the precincts of the House in anticipation of the division, could not be induced to sit through the speeches. A little fillip was given by Sir Charles Dilke's swift descent upon Sir M. H. Beach's slip about taxing tea. Bat, as there seemed no near prospect of Sir Michael and his friends having any control over events, nothing paiti- calar came of this. Mr. Gladstone was present early in the sitting. But he left at the dinner hour. and, contrary to his ' custom when he intends to make a speech, was absent for a considerable period. It seemed as though Mr. Childers' long and dull oration, followed by Sir Stafford Northcote's equally dull but happily less lengthy speech would close the debate. Then the division would be taken, the Govern- ment majority would be a little more or a little lees than usual, and on the next day bueiness would begin agais. Never as far as the g, eenest memory goes in the House of Commons was a great crisis allowed to creep on so abso- lutely unsuspected. Mr. Gladstone rose at a quarter to one in the morning, a course of late years most unusual with him. When he speaks in the House of Commons he always has before him a vision of the country listening for his words. He knows the physical difficulties in the way of transmitting an im- portant speech delivered at a late hour in the House of Commons, and invariably, when he has an important speech to deliver, makes it as soon after five o'clock as possible. I fancy he had, early in the evening, no intention of speak- ing, or he would have followed Sir Michael Beach. But at this time it began to dawn upon the Government whips that there were breakers ahead. Lord Richard Grosvenor came in whilst Sir Stafford Northcote was speaking, and held some moments earnest conversation with the Premier. It was after this that he rose and, late as was the hour, ill as he has been, made a speech, which for force of argument, felicity ef illustration, awl energy of delivery, ha n been rarely equalled even by himself. Still he utterly failed to raise the audience to any pitch of enthusiasm, or even of animation. The business which kept members up till this time was to vote. They knew how the division would go.

, 'Let them give their votes and go home. The division proceeded for some time with the same absence of suspicion of its import. Some members, eager to secure-a cab before the rush came, actually left the House as soon as they had given their vote, and only learned from the papers next morning that they had been assisting at a great historical crisis. The bustle, which presently grew into a state of mad excitement, began almost imperceptibly. There was a movement in the neighbourhood of Lord Randolph Churchill which betokened something. The noble lord excitedly twisted his moustache, and eagerly questioned late comers from the division lobby as to the state of the poll. When at twenty minutes to two Lord Kensington pushed his way through the throng at the Bar, the possibility that the Government had been beaten for the first time dawned upon the crowded House. For five years the Whip who has "told" the Opposi- .6•A forces has been the first to return. Since Lord Kensington was first in, it was plata that he had the fewest number to tell. Then the cheering, or rather the mad shouting, began below the gangway on the Conservative side. Lord Randolph Churchill's moustache suffered terribly. Had the suspense been further prolonged the occasion might have proved fatal to it. But when the paper was handed to Mr. Row- land Winn indicating that the Conservatives had gained the majority, Lord Randolph by a sudden impales sprung on to the bench, and waving his bat above his head, shouted like a madman. The example was followed by the Irish mem- bers, Mr. Healy greatly distiuguishipg himself, whilst Mr. Irligear, modestly keeping his seat, bellowed out "Buck- shot !,Buckshot I" at the top of his melodious voice. Meanwhile, Mr. Gladstone, who had begun to write his nightly letter to the Queen whilst members were returning - from the division lobbies, went on quietly writing as If nothing particular were going on about him. This dramatic scene was, of coarse, follows] by the resignation of the Ministry, and at the present moment the next movement is with the Queen. Her Majesty, with a fatality that has lately pursued her holiday movements, happens again, for the third time within a few weeks, to be absent from tht neighbourbeod of the metropolis at the time of a great national crisis,. This has already caused undesir- able delay in completing the arrangements. But there is little doubt that to-morrow night Mr. Gladstone will be able to pat in plain English the enigmatical communication =made to the House of Cemmous on Tuesday, and inform the ..House that he has resigned office and that Lord Salisbury has been sent for. There is some talk of Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues being induced to continue in office. But that is simply impossible. It is scarcely any secret,,and it is a fact within my personal knowledge derived from the highest authority that if the Government had not beerrbeaten in the division on Tuesday morning the Cabinet would have been broken up on Wednesday by the retirement of Sir C. Mike and Mr. Chamberlain. Efforts made at the Cabinet Council on Mondayto find a model vivendi on the question of the renewal of the Coercion Act absolutely failed, and there remained for consideration only the way ,and the hour at which the resignations should be announced. The decision of the House on Tuesday WAS a happy deliverance of the Cabinet from a difficult position, and they are not likely, saving been thus fortuitously delivered, voluntarily to put •their necks in the yoke again. We shill have a C"serva- tive Ministry for five militate and then a Liberal Govern- ment stronger than ever. Lord Coleridge probably wishes that the Adams case had been settled six months ago on the basis which has now , withdrawn it from the range of public conversation. From first to Last it has been an unfortunate business, and may now be buried with supreme satisfaction. The next thing we are likely to hear of the case is that Miss Coleridge is 'Mrs. Adams, and that, as in the old story books, they lived happily together ever afterwards. The arrangement come to was, I believe, based noon an understanding which ex- isted with respect to Lord Coleridge's disposition of his property. ,It was understood that Miss Coleridge had origi- nally been named in her father's will for the sum of £14,000. Upon the quarrel ensuing she had been struck out of the will. Overtures were a week ago made proposing to rein- date her in her former position if all legal proceedings were .stopped. A noire favourable arrangement was finally made, Lord Coleridae paying an annuity of six hundred a year to his daughter, which will enable her comfortably to set up in housekeeping. Besides this she will, eventually, come in for the lump sum of which the annuity represents the in- terest. London Society is poorer by the absence of the Marquis of Queensbury„ who has just left his old haunts for America. The Marquis, who married early, has a son in the navy. He is just now stationed at Vancouyers Island, and thither the Marquis is proceeding. Afterwards he will go a-ranching, •the favourite holiday occupation of noble lords in these days. Very little has been heard of "young Q" of late years, though the family reputation has been kept up by his sister, Lady Florence DiKie, whose famous escapade with a rnysterieos stranger from whose murderous hands she was saved only by the sagacity of her de, will not have faded from public memory. The last time I saw the Marquis of Queensbury be was leaking for the Editor of the Times That journal had printed a letter over his signature in which a luckless compositor had made a very comical blunder. The Marquis held the Editor personally respon- aible for this, and had once or twice called upon him at the office. But by a strange coincidence Mr. Chinnery (in whose days the incident happened) wao never in when the Idarquis called. In his hot youth the Marquis was a fair average boxer, and as a patron of the ring his name Will live /or ever in connection with what are known as "the Queensberry Rules." There is something very terrible going to happen to the R.A. The academy is getting quite unacademic. Those tscratches on the pictures were bad omens and did not appear for nothing. A. Cold bleeuled critic indeed said that some parsimenious visitor would not buy a catalegae, and being uot only stingy but also abeent-minciwd marked the pictures instead of the book. The sane critic suggested that if the academicians were discontented, the remedy was in their ewe had. They hart only to hang their pictures high up well above the line and out of harm's reach, leaving the outsiders in this post of danger. But the R.A's. won't do My such thing. And now their decline and fall is brought within measurable distance. They have actually elected Mr. Brune Jones an associate, and they have rushed iiripetu- -4,181Y on their destruction; for, though three candidates were up he was chosen by a big majority. Years ago when ha was painting his best pictures, he used to send in to Trafalgaroquare, but they would not hang him. Then he sulked. I don't nee the word invidiously. When genius is thrust aside to admit mediocrity Balking is always a virtue. Be stuck to the grand school which he bad followed from the first. He painted DO pot boilers, nor subjects for the photographer. And now in his old age he ranks after the young men who during the last few years have taken the .3Catlen by storm.
Xetters to the eCtilor.
A PILL TO PURGE NUISANCES.

Sir,—l noticed a short time ago one of your correspon- dents complaining of the nuisance arising from Longford Works. May Ibe permitted to point out a seemingly very simple, inexpensive, but effective, method et at least testing this as well as many other " nuisances " in which it is cur- rently stated our good old town abounds? Section 114 of the Public Health Act, 1875, which is the foundation of all municipal authority, after naming certain trades classified as "offensive," continues—" or any manu- factory or place used for any trade business procesi or manu- facture causing effluvia, is certified to any urban authority by their medical officer or by any two legally qualified medical practitioners, or by any ten inhabitants of the dis- trict of such urban authority, to be a nuisance or injurious to the health of any of the inhabitaats of the district, such urban authority shall direct complaint to be made before a justice, who may summon the person by or on whose behalf the trade is carried on to appear before a court of summary jurisdiction." Penalties range from 40s to £2OO en convic- tion. It would appear from this that the inhabitants of any town practically have the controlling power of nuisances in their own hands it they will exercise it, the wording of the Act making it imperative upon the authority to take action en such a certificate being lodged with them, for you will observe it states they "shall direct complaint to be made," rtc. I would therefore urge all who are suffering either in health or comfort from 4effensive trades" to 12th June,lBBs. COMBINE.

div.head: IHE DAWN OF HOPE.
div.p: IHE DAWN OF HOPE.

Sir,—After years— of mistaken policy our rulers seem at I length awakened to the indispatable fact that Ireland's I claim to equitable freedom can no longer be delayed. Ire- land has received from the hands of her rulers during this last •40 years many concessions, for which she has been, grateful, but no promised reform has called from her such a warm expression of joy as the intended Land Purchase Clause. The leaders of Irish opinion know the blessings such an Act would confer upon the people. Any measure having for its object the restoration of the land to the original holders of it will fix the sturdy peasant upon the soil of his forefathers, and restore an inheritance of which his race has so long been deprived. It redounds to the honour ef a Liberal Government to attempt, in the face of grave difficulties, to complete these Irish land reforms by such a beneficent measure. Yet for a nation like Ireland to enjoy such a blessing she must feel herself free. The great diminution of crime in Ireland has shown that the dawn of hope has already set in. She would seem to be rising from her long thraldom with a fixed determination to forget tha past ; and filled with hopes for the future. There should be no attempts to re- rivet the shackles of coercion upon the limbs of a free-born people. Never was there a more favourable opportunity afforded for an English Government to show that they can rule without force. Coercion laws, in times past, have driven the people into the arms of demagogues and truck- ling agitators rather than cause them to love or respect the administrators of the law. It is an insult to suggest that the sons of Erin are an inferior race. Have they not been found equal upon the battle field in the hour of England's danger? Have not her statesmen shed lustre upon the throne of England ? Has not the eloquence of her patriots been the admiration of the world? When called to duty, Ireland has shown that her loyalty is unquestionable. Why, then, .ehould her people be made to feel that they are aliens, ani that exceptional repressive laws are required to keep them in subj,ction ? The time is past for such dealings with a people who have proved themselves a tower of strength to England. Treat Ireland with justice and she will resprct and love you. But make the slightest step backwards from her path of progress, and she will reco 1 from your presence and con- tinue to foster her past hatred -of England. Hoping you will give this a place in your next issue, I remain, yours truly, June sth, 1885.
THOMAS .FLOOD.

THE PADGATE SCHOOLS. Sir,—Does it not seem as though the Board of Guardians have radically misconceived the uses and purposes of Pad- gate schools ? Some learned lexicographers define a school as a" place of education and improvement," but to judge by their discussions, the Guardians do not look upon the Padgate establishment as a place of this kind. They are ambitious, some of them tell us, to make this establishment a model of its kind —an example to other schools but when they come to consider the ways and means of doing this we find that they talk of such things as putting up a big clock, laying out new playgrounds, and of making accessible that hospital which has been so wonderfully isolated that very few even of the physically able have seen its interior, and those who have talk of their visit in something the same way as an adventurous tourist might talk of having climbed some high Alpine peak. If the Guardians think they are likely to get " model schools" by such means as these they must be mightily impressed with the value of mere externals. I should think if they gave more care and attention to " edu- cating and improving," mentally and physically, the youths under their charge the prospect of achieving their ambition would be better. The young inmates of Padgate schools have not been born with silver spoons in their mouths, and when they are thrust out into the world the "struggle for existence" will be a very real thing to them. Under these circumstances it ía clearly the first duty of the Guardians to fit, as tar as in them lies, their young proteges, by judicious bodily and mental training, to take a successful part in the struggle which is before them. Compared with this duty that of improving and beautifying the structural arrangements of the schools is very insignificant. If you do not consider it hypercritical, I should just like to mention one thing about the Guardians' way of doing business, which always strikes me when I read their dis- cussions, and that is the affectation of high moral motives of some of the Guardians. They do everything "on prin- ciple." If a medical arrangement is to be re-arranged it is to be done "on principle." If two or three partially white- washed paupers are to be removed from one place to another it is to be done "on principle," and the Christmas allow- 1 ance of beer to the inmates of the workhouse Is both sup- ported and opposed" on principle." Now why cannot they be content like other people with supporting or opposing proposals on the ground of their expediency or advisability without invoking principles every time they have to do a little bit of parochial work. Ills true the word "principle" is very much of the nature of a parrot-cry and does not as a rule convey any very defi- nite idea, but everybody understands a Principle to be fixed and continually operative. Now, if the Guardians make all these changes' on principle " they , must have been violating principles in a most flagrant manner before the changes were made. Their "vaulting ambition" to be highly moral in all they do lands them on the other side," and they might very wisely take the advise of Hamletana "reform it altogether." JAQUES.

div.head: GORDON VERSUS BRADLAUGH.
div.p: GORDON VERSUS BRADLAUGH.

Sir,—"Defender " seems to be a little put out on account of the way in which Mr. Bradlaugh dealt with General Gordon, during his recent visit to Karrington. I am Cur- prieed that your correspondent should presume to adopt the signature he has done' seeing that he wilfully allowed the opportunity to slip by him, wherein he might have done valiant work in defending General Gordon's memory. Both the chairman and Mr. Bradlaugh repeatedly invited those who had, questions to put or opposition to offer to step for- ward and do so, and I ara quite sure the audience, unlike , the generality of Tory audiences, would have listened patiently to any clear statement that might have been made. With the exception of one base and cowardly insinuation, I have little fault to fad with "Defender's" statement of his case. No doubt he would be struck with amazement, as a good portion of the audience were, to find the idol, so per- sistently worshipped by almost the whole nation, toppled over and broken into pieces. Hero weeship wants carefully watching, or it has a tendency to make fools of men, as witness the wonderful elevation of our one' General and his splendid achievements in the Soudan. Mr. Bradlaugh is charged with speaking adversely of General Gordon, because "he has a reputation to main- tain," and also because it would be impossible for him to "gild refined gold." Strange talk this, Mr. Editor; quite a new doctrine is here set forth, and no demist Mr. radlangh may find he has something to learn new that" Defender," eschewing the public platform, takes to the public press. Is it by telling the people unpalateable truths that a man gains popularity? Is a man denounced as a demagogue because he prefers to smash idols instead of smashing Mandi's ? If so, then Mr. Bradlaugh is all that " Daimler " makes bins out to be. As a matter of fact, Mr. Bradlaugh made no statement that he was not prepared to prove. In his hand he held chapter and verse for all he said, and if "Defen- der" thought he was wrenching quotations from their con- text his duty was to challenge the lecturer at once. I can assure "Defender" that this would have been nay course if I had to do It in the face of all the howling Tories yet remaining to Warrington. There seems to be a charming simplicity running through " Defender's " letter. floes he not see that this Christian hero seems to have devoted the whole of his life to thwart- ing the avowed object of Christ's mission on earth ? In- stead of teaching the people to "love one another," has he not on every occasion that offered itself taken sides with the oppressor, sold himself in fact to the aisle of might against tight. It is notorious, and subsequent events proved it, that this was the case in China ; and in the Soudan, it is quite clear that his presence proved a source of trouble to the Government, and was a curse to the Soudanese. In such portions of Gordon's diary as I have seen, it is stated that he could have left Khartoum any time during the first two months. Instead of doing this he set the orders of the Government at defiance, levied taxes on all surrounding tribes. Where there was no money he took cattle, where both cattle and =suer were gone he .took wives and mothers along with their children. These he sold .or gave away as slaves, their husbands and fathers he made into soldiers. This is no fanciful statement, but is gathered from his own writings. Dues "Defender " forget the thrill that ran through England when Gordon sent word hems that it Iwould not be policy for his mission to have for its object the liberation of the slaves I e came in contact with. Nay, , did he not demand that the British Government should ap- point and take into its pay the Prince of Slave-dealers, Zebehr Pasha? I ask " Defender " where was Cheistian principle in this? Did not Gordon promulgate a proclamation in which was shown that, while Gordon thought slavers' wars made for the purpose of taking slaves, were detestable, he did not see any objection to the sale of a child where the parents and the child of their own free will agreed to it! Gordon dis- tinctly states himself that he captured eeven slave dealere, ,

and took their slaves from them, and while the men were put into the ranks of his army, the women were told a to be the wives of his soldiers. This brings me to the base insinuation made by " Defen- der " against Mr. Bradlaugh. He says this "seems to be a startling application of the doctrine of free-love Mr. Brad- laugh is said to be theoretically if not practically enamoured of." I ask what is intended to be conveyed in this passage? In what portion of his writings has be given grounds for this impression ? In what speech is it conveyed that he is en- amoured of an immoral life of this kind 7 Surely if he was so much in love with it, some record would appear as wit- ness against him. But my chief reason for taking notice of "Defender's" letter is to point out the fearful responsibility England un- dertakes in encouraging this war fever. The latter state of Jingoism is worse than the former, and it is noticeable that, while the clergy of England gave a tacit consent to Beacons- field's Jingoism, they have madly urged on all its worst symptoms during the past two years. The Pall Mall Gaz- ette, writing on this subject, says, "What have our clergy done to remind England in this great crisis of the impor- tance of being on their guard against the promptings of passion, and of bringing to the decision of the greatest questions that can confront a nation the most careful and Impartial judgment and the most anxious desire to ascertain the whole truth, and not to take a single important step under the influence of popular excitement or national ani- mosity? What have they dons? They have been dumb dogs all." It remains but for me to point out that the Radical party stands preeminent to-day as the only party actively engaged in pleading for peace, in the Radical press. The Egyptian war has been repeatedly denounced. On the Radical plat- form none have urged more than Mr. Bradlaugh that the "greatest of British interests is peace." Two years ago the Rev. Thomas Ripon writing to John Bright, questioned the right hon. gentleman respecting " peace at any price," from an abstract point of view, and he received for answer the following respecting the Egyptian war :—" I will not dis- cuss the abstract question. . . But of this war I may say this, that it has no better jestification than other ware which have gone before it, and that doubtless when the blood is shed and the cost pal I, and the results seen and weighed, we shall be generally of that opinion. Perhaps the bondholders, and those who have made money by it, and those who have got promotion and titles and pensions, will defend it, but thoughtful and Christian men will con- demn it." Weighed in John Bright's scales, where are the Christian men ? Charles Bradlaugh early saw that, to quote from the Manchester Examiner, which, speaking of the Soudanese, says :—" These men are engaged in no re- volt, and are not rebels," consequently be spoke out fear- lessly, and doing this deserves the Oanks of all who have courage enough to shake off prejudice. Ido not purpose saying more in answer to " Defender," for I am sure that he, like myself, would scarcely call those who, unbidden, rush into war—men of peace. We may reasonably hope that the new constituencies will refuse to elect men whose object in life seems to be that of keeping the nation in a state of turmoil. In the present Parliament the fighting interest is represented by 108 members, and there are 272 members connected with the Peerage. No wonder the people are kicked about like footballs. CAPTAIN CUTTLE. June 3rd, 1885.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JUNE 13, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JUNE 13, 1885.

stating that Lord Salisbury had arrived there at 7.20 on Friday morning, whilst despatchea front other parts along the route positively asserted that his Lordship was not a passer.ger by the train in question. All doubt upon the sub- ject was, however, set at rest on official authority during the morning, and by the receipt of frequent telegrams describing his progress to the North. His Lordship break- fasted at Perth, reached Aberdeen at a quarter-past two and finished his railway journey at Ballater at a quar- ter to four, travelling in the last section in a special Train ordered by Lord Bridport by Her Majesty's orders. From Banger Lord Salisbury proceeded in one of the Royal car- riages, finally reaching Balmoral Castle at five o'clock. It has transpired that Lord Salisbury did not redeive the tele- gram conveying Her Majesty's commands until about seven o'clock on Thursday evening, when he was dining with the Dowager Duchess of Marlborough and her son Lord Ran- dolph Churchill. This circumstance is of course accepted as conclusive proof, that Lord Salisbury at any rate has not been affected by the persistent efforts of certain prominent Conservatives to dasia.ge Lord Churchill's chances of a seat in the new cabinet. There is very little doubt felt in qaar- tete usually well informed as to Lord Salisbury's intention to take office. Little credit is given to the reports current again to-day that his lordship will make it a sins qua nen of his acceptance of office that the Liberal party shall assist the new Government in passing a Crimes Act for Ireland It is not considered likely that such a pledge would be given, and it is not easy to specify what guarantee could be given for the fulfillment of promises of such a character. Both Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote are confi- dent that if they find on inquiry that the renewal of the present Crimes Act in some shape or form be really neces- sary for the preservation of order in Ireland they will re- ceive the support ef the bulk of the moderate Liberal party, in addition to that of their own party supporters. With the exception of this bill, the new Government will not attempt to carry any measures of a contentious character, and the hope is therefore expressed in Conservative circles that it may be possible to finish all indispensible business by the end of July. Mr. Parnell, however, has caused it to be in- timated that he and his followers will oppose by every form ef the House any attempt to re-enact the Crimes Act in any shape or form, and Parliamentary 'strategists declare that the Parnellites will in that event have very little difficulty indeed in prolonging the session even to the last week in August or the first week in September. Moreover, the Irish party have arranged to support their action in Parliament by a rigorous anti-coercion campaign in Ireland. The Government will therefore have serious difficulties to con- tend with at the very outset, which they will scarcely be able to overcome without the assistance of a considerable proportion of the Liberal party in the House of Commons.

div.head: POLITICAL CRISIS. LORD SALISBURY SENT FOR.-EARLY RE FURN
div.p: THE POLITICAL CRISIS. LORD SALISBURY SENT FOR.-EARLY RE FURN
OF THE QUEEN.

- The following Intimation was conveyed in Thursday night's Court Circular IMO] Balmoral :—" In consequence of the state of political affairs her Majesty's departure from Balmoral, which was fixed for the 19th inst., will take place at as early a data as can be arranged." The Daily News says :—lt is known that if her Majesty consulted her own convenience she would prefer not to re- turn from Balmoral to Windsor till after the Ascot week In the meantime, her Majesty has summoned Lord Salisbury to Balmoral, and he left London for that destination by the nine o'clock train on Thursday night from King's Cross. Before taking this step her Majesty had in all probability assured hersed by telegraph communication that Mr. Gladstone was not disposed to withdraw his resignation ; and in that event the Sovereign considered that she had no alternative but to seed for the Leader of the Opposition. Opinions are still divided as to whether Lord Salisbury will consent, under the peculiar circumstances of the case, to accept office. The summons received by Lord Hartington early on Wednesday evening directing him to go to Balmoral—a summons withdrawn by a later message—bus given rise to snarly speculations. The suggestion of Lord Hartington's visit came in the first instance from Mr. Gladstone, who thought it would be convenient for Lord Hartington to be on the spot to afford any explanation that might be re- quired by her Majesty. The Queen in the first instance approved the suggestion; but having decided to return• t 3 Windsor, relieved Lord Hartington from the necessity of the joarnev.

A correspondent telegraphs from Balmoral :—Arrange- merits have just been completed for the departure of the Queen from Balmoral on Tuesday. Her Majesty will travel by the usual route, arriving at Windsor on Wednesday morning. Packing has already commenced in Downing-street. Mr. Gladstone has no other town house, and it is not his inten- tion to take one for what remains of the session.

In Conservative circles it is expected that if Lord Salis- bury becomes Prime Minister, Lord Carnarvon will be ap- pointed Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. In that event Sir Michael Hicks-Beach would return to the Colonial Office. It is stated that Mr. Gibson will be Lord Chan- cellor of Ireland. Trae withdrawal from the home of Corn. moos of one of the most energetic debaters on the Front Bench does not appear probable. But it is explained that the appointment need not necessarily he a permanent one. It carries with it, after whatever brief tenure of office, a life pension of £3,500, and there is no reason why, when the new Parliament comes in, Mr. Gibson should not re- sume his old place on the Front Opposition Bench. With the consent of both parties, the period of the ad- journment pending the completion of Ministerial re-elec- tions will be arranged se that no harm shall accrue to the Seats Bill.

The Press Association says :—There is some reason to expect that the Prime Minister will be prevailed upon to resume office upon the understanding that his Government should not be expected to undertake any coercive legisla- tion for Ireland. This condition might probably involve the resignation of the Viceroyalty of Ireland by Earl Spencer, but it would by no means lead to such a break up of the Liberal Cabinet as has been generally supposed. Mr. Gladstone is in entire agreement with Sir Charles Dilke and Mr. Chamberlain in the views they are known to hold upon that subject, and Mr. Trevelyan, although a former Chief Secretary for Ireland, is stated to have been converted at last Cabinet meeting to the same view. There is also rea- son to believe that Lord Northbrook, Lord Kimberley, Lord Derby, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, and the Marquis of Hartingtoo, as well probably as the Lord Chancellor, Lord Carlingford, Sir W. Harcourt, and Lord Rosebery would consent to re- join the Cabinet on the undertaking that the ordinary law should be relied upon as sufficient for the preservation of order in Ireland until the assembling of the reformed Par- liament, especially in view of the fact that during the in- terim the Irish people, like those of Great Britain, would be busily engaged with electioneering. It is not, however, expected that matters can reach this stage for at least a fortnight, and there is little likelihood that whatever ar- rangement may be made the House of Commons will be able to settle down again to ordinary business much before the close of the present month. Meantime the Ministerial crisis continues to be discussed on all hands with unabated interest, and politicians are I everywhere absorbed in keen speculations. Lord Harting- ton and several other colleagues of Mr. Gladstone called on Thursday afternoon at Downing-street, where telegrams and letters continue to pour in from leading politicians in almost every part of the country with reference to the poli- tical situation. Sir Richard Cross and Mr. W. H. Smith had interviews with Sir Stafford Northcote on Thursday morning, as had also Mr. Rowland Winn, the senior Con- servative whip, who had previously an interview with LOrEi Salisbury at Arlington-street. The Carlton Club, the Beaconsfield Club, the Reform Club, the National Liberal Club, and similar institutions were largely attended all day, and active politicians connected with these resorts were eagerly consulted by members and others concerning the probable outcome of the crisis. In view of what is at least the early possibility of the accession of the Conservative party to power, special significance is attached to the fact that Lord Randolph Churchill excused himself from his engagement to speak at the Beaconsfield Club House dinner on Thursday night, and that Mr. W. H. Smith, probably for similar reasons, thought it expedient not to deliver the poli- tical address which he had been Innounced to deliver on Thursday evening at Sndbury. The Ediohurgh correspondent of the Central News tele- graphed on Friday morning :—Lord Salisbury arrived at the Waverley Station. Edinburgh, at 6.20. and after a stop- page ef 20 minutes the train proceeded to the north. his lordship travelled in a first-class compartment, and was re- cognised by those about the station, but there was no de- monstration..
