The messenger who was &snatched to 13—kim—o-ra.l on Tuesday, with the dutiful communicition of the Cabinet, returned to London on Friday morning, with her Majeqty's r.ply which his now been placd in the hands of the Prime

Minister. It is understood that the Queen had received and would consii.r the proposed resignstion, and had mean- time cxlled urym Lord Salisbury to proceed to Balmoral and advise her as to his view of the political situation.

div.head: LATEST DETAILS.
div.p: LATEST DETAILS.

IThe Central News, telegraphing last night, says:—Much satiefaction is expressed in political circles, both Liberal and Conservative, at the decision of der Majesty to sum- , Mil Lord Salisbury to Balmoral. It was felt that the crisis had already lasted sufficiently long in an acute form, and the departure of the leader of the Opposition for Scotland has had the effect of greatly relaxing the political tension which has existed throughout the week. Considerable and apparently quite unnecessary mystery attended the depar- ture of Lord Salisbury. All information on the subject was positively refused by OA party efficials, and even on Friday morning members of his Lordship's honaehold positively asserted that be had not left London. The mystery was increased by the receipt Of a telegram from Edinburgh

div.head: TEST NEWS.
div.p: LA TEST NEWS.

The first sham fight of the season was fought at Aldershot an Friday morning under the superintendence of Generals Anderson and Cooper. It is officially announced that Vice-Admiral Prince of Leiningen has been selected to succeed Admiral Corbett as commander-in•chief at the Nore. Mr. Michael Davitt, has been inundated with letters from persons in all parts of Ireland and Great Britain congra- tulating him on the completion of his ticket of leave. It now appears, however, that the event will not be an ac- complished fact till the 17th of next month. GESERAL GRANT.—General Grant's condition is un- changed, excepting that of late he complains of sleepless- ness—chiefly caused Ley the mental strain resulting from several hours' daily labour upon his book. This work is finished, says that the final proofs have still to be cor- rected.

IRISH WEDDING GIFT TO PRINCESS BEATRICE. The ladies of County Waterford, headed by the Marchioness of Waterford, have decided to present a wedding gift to H.R.H. Princess Beatrice on her marriage with Prince Henry of Battenburg, in the shape of a fan of Cappoquin lace mounted in mother of pearl. THE LISWOUTII COLLIERY DISASTER.—At Gateshead on Friday a charge was preferred against the owners of the Usworth Colliery, the scene of a recent fatal mining disas- ter, of having permitted shot firing at the time, in contra- vention of the Act of Parliament. The magistrates, after hearing Mr. Willis, Government inspector, and several min- ing engineers, adjourned the case sine die, in order to obtain the opinion of the Queen's Bench whether the rules had been complied with. FRIGHTFUL FLY-WHEEL ACCIDENT.—On Friday morning the fly-wheel of an engine at the Stock-lane Spinning Company's mill, Oldham, flow off, sections of it going through the roof and demolishing part of the mill. A boy named Edgar Norcross was buried beneath the ruins, and after a search was discovered. He was seriously irijured and removed to Oldham Infirmary. Search is being pro- secuted amongst the debris, and it is feared other persons are buried. _ .

TERRIBLE Surma —At an inquest which was held on Friday at Hart's Hill, near Dudley, it was shown that a tradesman, named William Harris. had committed suicide In a most determined manner. Whilst in a desponding mood, the deceased, with a razor, nearly severed his head from his body. When found, the razor was in the deceased's hand. The head was hanging at the back of the body. A verdict to the effect that the deceased committed Autcide during temporary insanity was returned. THE GORDON MEMORIAL.—A meeting in aid of Gordon Boys' Camp was held on Friday, in the Prince's Hall, Lon- don, the Lord Mayor presiding. Among the subscriptions were £lOO from the Duke of Bedford, £65 from Eton boys. A letter from Mies Gordon was read, warmly approving of the scheme. The speakers, who included the Dean of West- minster, Mr. Thomas Hughes, Lord Napier of Magdala, Lord Shaftesbury, Cardinal Manning, Archdeacon Farrar. and Sir Hardinge Giffard, all agreed that the various Gor- don memorials should be amalgamated, and that the Boys' Camp was best.
DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT THE SOUTH KENSING. TON MUSEUM.

A fire, which at one time threatened to assume most alarming proportions, broke out in the Indian Section of the South Kensington Museum shortly arter noon to-day, and resulted in the total destruction of what is known as the French Annexe of the Indian Museum. This building occupies a position on the same plot of land upon which the International Inventions Exhibition is situated, and the rumour rapidly spread throughout the length and breadth of London that the "Inventories" was on 'fire. The fire was first discovered at the eastern end of the roof of the Indiam Museum, and the Royal Engineers Fire Brigade I was quickly on the spot, but could do no good is subduing the flames in consequence of the difficulty of procuring a supply of water. A numer- rous contingent of the Metropolitan Fire Brigade, under the command of Captain Shaw, was quickly on the spot, and desperate efforts were at once made to save the Exhibition and the surrounding buildings. No less than 13 of the fire brigade engines were rapidly brought into play, and these received valuable assistance from a number of private hydrants. Many thousands of people of course col- lected around the burning structure, and it was with the greatest difficulty that the police succeeded in keeping back the public. Amongst the first to arrive at the scene were the Prince and Princess of Wales and the Duke of Cambridge. The Prince of Wales, who has taken so great an interest in the Exhibition, was apparently much excited, but was considerably relieved after he had been conducted all round the burning fire by Captain Shaw, who expressed his confident opinion that his men would be well able to save the exhibition. The French annexe of the Indian Museum was, however, totally destroyed, although, hap- pily, the most valuable specimens exhibited therein were removed before they were seriously damaged by either fire or water. No one was seriously hurt in connection with the fire, but a few people sustained slight Cuts from the splin- ters of the hand grenades.

div.head: GREAT FIRE IN HAYTI.
div.p: GREAT FIRE IN HAYTI.

NEW YORK, TRURSDAY.—lntelligence received here an- nounces that a great fire has occurred at Les Cares, Hayti, by which 100 buildiorrs were destroyed and 1,000 persons rendered homeless. The loss is estimated at 2,000,000 dollars. THE POPE AND THE IRISH BISHOPS Rom, FRIDAY.—The Pope yesterday sanctioned the de- cisions arrived at by the Irish Bishops daring their recent meetings at the Propaganda. His Holiness also approved the programme for the meeting which the Irish prelates will shortly hold in Dublin. This programme accords en- tirely with the resolutions adopted at the propaganda.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. __
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. __
The House met F-t-ti;;;O Woo):

THE MINISTERIAL CRISIS —Lord GIIANVILLE said : I have now to inform your lordships that Mr. Gladstone ten- dered his resignation and that of his colleagues to Her Majesty who has been graciously pleased to accept it, and to send for Lori Salisbury who is at this moment at Bal- moral. Under these circumstances, we shall not proceed with any of the ordinary business, except the Redistribu- tion Bill.—Lord KIMBERLEY, in asking their lordships to consider repod of amendmeat to the Redistribution Bill, saicj he had the full concurrence of Lord Salisbury. A new Manse bad been introduced providing that elections should take place after the let of November.—Lord CRA.NREtOOK, on behalf of Lord SAisbury, consenting. the report was agreed to, and the Bill was read a third time.—The House then adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at four o'clock. There was a very full attendance of members when the Speaker took the chair. Sir M. Beach and Mr. Gibson were the first to take their seats on the front Opposition bench. They were soon afterwards joined by Lord R. Churchill, James Lowther, Sir W. Hart Dyke, Lord John Manners, and Sir R. Cross. Sir S. Northcote entered at 25 past four' and wis received with cheers. On the Ministerial bench were Mr, Chamberlain. Mr. Childers, Mr. G. Russell, and Mr. Ashley. When Lord R. Grosvenor entered he was re- ceived with cheers. lie was followed by Sir C. Duke, and at half-past four Mr. Gladstone entered the House, and was received with very loud cheers.

TEM RESIGNATION OF THE GOVERNMENT. After a tevr notices of motion bad been given, Mr. GrAneyousi rose, and was again loudly cheered. He said he wished to communicate to the House what had taken place since he informed it that the Cabinet had made a dutiful communication to her Majesty. The communica- tion, it was perfectly understood, was the resigration of the Cabinet. The communication was sent to Bilmoral on the 6th; it reached on:the 100, and on the 11th a communi- lion was received from her Majesty stating that she accepted the resignation tendered and that she bad sent for Lord Salisbury. He stated that

the resignation arose out of the vote on Tuesday. He had nothing further to state than that Lord Salisbury left town last night, and, under these circumstances, it was impossible for him to have communication with him. In ordinary circumstances, he should have moved that the House at its rising should adjourn until Monday, but there was mentioned on Tuesday the Redistribution Bill. It was necessary that that Bill should be censidered and com- pleted as early possible and it was now being considered by the House of Lords. There were no serious differences likely to arise, and therefore be respectfully suggested that the amendments might be considered that evening.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE quite agreed that the Bill should proceed as rapidly as possible. The amendments were not yet printed, and from communications he had received he doubted whether they could be considered that evening.—The sitting of the House was than suspended. • At ten minutes past five the Redistribution Bill was brought from the House of Lords —Sir C. DILE& moved that the amendments be printed and considered on Monday next.—This was agreed to and the House at a quarter past five adjourned until Monday.
RUNCORN AND WIDNES. STRANGE CONDUCT OF A RUNCORN MAN.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday morning, be- fore Messrs. James Handley and G. L. Davies, a man named Abel Cooper West was brought up under warrant, charged with using certain threats towards Ann West, his wife, from which she was afraid he would do her some bodily in- jury.—The complainant said she Jived at 17, Vine-street, and had been married to the prisoner eleven years. When she married him he was 22 years of age, and she was 31. When working the prisoner was a labourer at the docks. Lately the prisoner had often threatened that he would hang for her, that he would not own her for his wife, and that he would not work for her any more. A week ago he got hold of her by the throat. She could see the "savage" in him, and went out of the house, not daring to go in again that night. She had been a " throrough good wife" to the prisoner, and had a clean home for him. The prisoner was not working now, and said he would not work any more.— In reply to Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, as to bow the prisoner was kept, the complainant said that she had a bit of money, but it was nearly done. She was try- ing to kept the house open to keep the prisoner, she supposed, to walk about. On Thursday he said be would sell her up, and put her in the workhouse.— Mr. Johnson: You said something about seeing a change in his condition. What do you mean by that? Well, he is going after a lot of young ladies in the town, and says he will not have me for his wife: I think his head is affec- ted by it.—Mr. Davies : How long is it since be worked? Very nearly three years.—The Chairman : You have never suffered any violence at his hands? Yee; I have had black flesh and black eyes from hini.--The prisoner (to his wife) : Did I threaten you on Thursday night? Yes.— Didn't that fancy lodger of yours--. He is not my fancy lodger. I am a respectable, decent woman.—Didn't the lodger knock me down, and didn't you say "kill him ?" No.—Didn't you give me a black eye? No, the roughs out- side did that.—Didn't you follow the lodger 'out at ten o'clock, and say you would go with him? No, I did not; I was at Bazley's.—Did I hit you ? Yes.—The prisoner: When? Last week ; because I would not give you money. —Would it have killed a fly when I hit you? Yes. You asked me for a penny for shaving.—The prisoner : I never threatened you since I had you.—Witness : You said you, would be hung for me, and would sell me up and put me in the Workhouse. I have been a good wife to you. The prisoner, made a statement to the effect that he had been " thumped " by the lodger.— Clara Littlemore, wife of James Littlemore, living in Vine- street, said on Thursday night she went to Mrs West's house. The prisoner was then on the floor. The lodger, a man named Rigby, was also on the floor, and it appeared that a struggle had taken place, and was just over. She thought they were just parting. She was afraid and walked out, and a large crowd collected round the door.—Mr. Johnson I inquired whether there was any doubt as to the state of the prisoner's mind 7—Superintendent Leah replied that he had received several complaints about the prisoner. The lodger referred to had been to the police.station twice, as well as Mrs West. Other people had complained of his conduct both at home and abroad. Personally be knew nothing of his conduct, except what he beard from other people.—Mr. Johnson (to Mrs West) : Have you any idea that he does not know what he is tieing? The com- plainant : lam certain be does not. It is in the blood. He has a sister in the asylum.—The complainant signed an in. formation to the effect that her husband was a lunatic, and not under proper control.—The case was adjourned for an hour to allow an opportunity for a medical examination, and on the resumption of the case Dr. Mangan was called. He stated that the prisoner was rather peculiar, but there was no sign of insanity. He did not think he would be justified in signing a certificate which would commit the prisoner to a lunatic asylum.—The Chairman said the case would, therefore, have to be dealt with in the ordinary way. —The prisoner said he had nothing to say except that he had never threatened his wife.—The magistrates ordered the prisoner to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and two sureties in £lO each, or a month's bard labour.— The prisoner : It's a " rum " thing. I never had to find bail before.—lnspector Roche observed that the prisoner had no friends or relations in Runcorn except Mr. Pegg, a beer' house keeper, who was a cousin, and he had refused to go bail for the prisoner.—The case excited much interest, the prisoner being well known through his very singular con- duct in the streets for some months past, and a large crowd witneesed his departure for Knutsford.

div.head: WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.

Last evening the 18th annual festival of the Widnes Athletic Club was commenced in the show field, Faraworth, under very propitious circumstances. A day of almost tropical heat gave place to an evening sunny, cool, and pleasant, and a concourse of several thousand spectators gathered round the ring. As usual, the sports were under the laws of the Amateur Athletic Association, and the judges were Messrs. E. Bolton, E. A. Chorlton, T. T. Matthieson, A. McClennan, and H. S. Tinamis. Mr. Walter Platt per- formed the duties of handicapper, official time keeper, and referee; and Mr. T. Wilkinson eilciated as starter. The events of last evening were all of local interest. competi- tors being expected to reside within a limited area of the village of Farnworth. The entries were, however, an increase upon previous years, no less than 180 athletes having sent in their names for the various competitions. But Saturday is the great occasion when people frera all parts of the north of England as- semble in their thousands to watch some of the finest ama- teur athletes in the country battle for supremacy, and to- day there will be no lack of attraction. J. M. Cowie, of the London Athletic Club, L. E. Myers. of Manhattan, and W. Snooks, of Moseley Harriers, all champion fiat racers will coMpetsi, and the sport promises to be of superior ex- cellence. div.head: NEWTON RACES.
div.p: NEWTON RACES.

These races command the support and patronage of a large district, and as the meeting, which formerly extended over three days, is cut down to two, the sport ought at least to equal that of former times. The course has been in splen- did order, but neither the Manor Cup nor the Newton Cup com- mands the interest they used to do, and considerable uncer- tainty prevailed as to what would compete for the latter race. A pretty large audience, however, was well assured for the meeting, which commenced on Thursday, as the trains from Doncaster on Wednesday night were crowded, and those who took time by the forelock and travelled by the ordinary train to Manchester had the mortification of seeing the specials, which started some time later, give them the go-by at Penistene. The arrivals were not so numerous as usual on the eve of the Newton Meetings, and the fixture bad evidently surf dred froth being placed to follow Don- caster.
